arXiv:2507.00425v1 [cs.LG] 01 Jul 2025

Flexible Language Modeling in Continuous Space with Transformer-based Autoregressive Flows

Ruixiang Zhang    Shuangfei Zhai    Jiatao Gu    Yizhe Zhang    Huangjie Zheng    Tianrong Chen Affiliation: [1mm] Miguel Angel Bautista, Josh Susskind, Navdeep Jaitly Affiliation: [1mm] Apple Affiliation: [1mm] {ruixiangz, szhai, njaitly}@apple.com
Abstract

Autoregressive models have driven remarkable progress in language modeling. Their foundational reliance on discrete tokens, unidirectional context, and single-pass decoding, while central to their success, also inspires the exploration of a design space that could offer new axes of modeling flexibility. In this work, we explore an alternative paradigm, shifting language modeling from a discrete token space to a continuous latent space. We propose a novel framework TarFlowLM, that employs transformer-based autoregressive normalizing flows [71] to model these continuous representations. This approach unlocks substantial flexibility, enabling the construction of models that can capture global bi-directional context through stacked, alternating-direction autoregressive transformations, support block-wise generation with flexible token patch sizes, and facilitate a hierarchical multi-pass generation process. We further propose new mixture-based coupling transformations designed to capture complex dependencies within the latent space shaped by discrete data, and demonstrate theoretical connections to conventional discrete autoregressive models. Extensive experiments on language modeling benchmarks demonstrate strong likelihood performance and highlight the flexible modeling capabilities inherent in our framework.

1 Introduction

Transformer-based autoregressive models [66, 5] have emerged as the dominant paradigm for language modeling, achieving remarkable performance by predicting discrete tokens one at a time under the cross-entropy objective. By scaling both model size and training data, these models excel at next-token prediction and have become the foundation for modern natural language generation systems.

Their remarkable success provides a strong foundation and inspires further exploration into the design space of autoregressive sequence modelling. While the established paradigm of discrete, typically unidirectional autoregressive generation offers a powerful and well-understood framework, we consider whether alternative formulations might offer new dimensions of flexibility and open different avenues for model construction. This work investigates such a possibility: What if autoregressive language modeling were reformulated within a continuous latent space? Moving to continuous representations allows for the preservation of the sequential factorization familiar from autoregressive methods, while potentially unlocking new modeling capabilities.

This adoption of continuous latent spaces is a direction also pursued by other generative frameworks; for instance, diffusion models have demonstrated strong capabilities in this domain. Our investigation, however, distinguishes itself by concentrating on autoregressive normalizing flows for modeling the joint distribution of these continuous sequences. We pursue this specific avenue because normalizing flows offer expressive power for density estimation, and critically, their intrinsic sequential processing aligns them closely with the fundamental mechanisms of discrete autoregressive language models. This alignment provides a unique vantage point: it allows us to explore how the core principles of autoregressive modeling can be evolved and potentially augmented when transitioned into a continuous, learnable transformation framework, thereby seeking to extend and enrich this successful paradigm.

Building on this perspective, we propose a novel framework that employs Transformer-based autoregressive normalizing flows [71] to model these continuous latent representations. This shift from discrete token space to a continuous latent space is key to unlocking substantial modeling flexibility. Our formulation facilitates the construction of models capable of capturing global bi-directional context through stacked, alternating-direction autoregressive transformations. It also supports block-wise generation with adaptable token patch sizes and enables a hierarchical multi-pass generation process, allowing for the observation and influence of sequence formation through intermediate stages. These capabilities arise naturally from the continuous and invertible nature of the flow-based transformations.

To this end, we present TarFlowLM, a Transformer-based Auto-Regressive Flow Language Model that uses mixture-based coupling transformations to effectively model the complex, multi-modal distributions created when mapping discrete data to a continuous latent space. Our key theoretical contribution is establishing the equivalence that transforms these mixture distributions into exact, invertible normalizing flow layers. Specifically, we show that a single-dimensional Mixture of Gaussians (MoG) distribution can be realized as a 1D Mixture-CDF flow, and a multi-dimensional MoG distribution as a Mixture-Rosenblatt flow. We also draw theoretical links between our continuous approach and standard discrete autoregressive models. Experiments on language modeling benchmarks show that our method achieves strong likelihood performance and, importantly, enables greater modeling flexibility. Our work expands the possibilities of language modeling by extending autoregressive methods into the continuous domain.

2 Background

Normalizing flows offer a method for constructing flexible probability distributions over continuous variables [51]. The core idea is to start with a simple base distribution pbase​(𝐮)p_{\text{base}}({\mathbf{u}}) defined on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, often a standard Gaussian, and transform samples 𝐮∼pbase​(𝐮){\mathbf{u}}\sim p_{\text{base}}({\mathbf{u}}) using an invertible and differentiable function f:ℝd→ℝdf:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}, known as a diffeomorphism. This process yields a variable 𝐳=f−1​(𝐮){\mathbf{z}}=f^{-1}({\mathbf{u}}) that follows a potentially much more complex distribution p⁡(𝐳)p({\mathbf{z}}). A key advantage of this approach is that the probability density function p⁡(𝐳)p({\mathbf{z}}) can be computed exactly using the change of variables formula:

log⁡p⁡(𝐳)=log⁡pbase​(f⁡(𝐳))+log⁡|detJf​(𝐳)|\log p({\mathbf{z}})=\log p_{\text{base}}(f({\mathbf{z}}))+\log\left|\det J_{f}({\mathbf{z}})\right| (1)

Here, Jf​(𝐳)J_{f}({\mathbf{z}}) is the Jacobian matrix of the transformation ff evaluated at 𝐳{\mathbf{z}}, and |det(⋅)||\det(\cdot)| denotes the absolute value of the determinant. Complex distributions are typically modeled by composing multiple simple transformations f=f(L)∘⋯∘f(1)f=f^{(L)}\circ\dots\circ f^{(1)}, where each layer f(ℓ)f^{(\ell)} is designed to be easily invertible and have a tractable Jacobian determinant. The log-density then becomes a sum of log-determinant terms from each layer, plus the log-density of the final transformed variable under the base distribution:

log⁡p⁡(𝐳)=log⁡pbase​(𝐮)+∑ℓ=1Llog⁡|detJf(ℓ)​(𝐡(ℓ−1))|\log p({\mathbf{z}})=\log p_{\text{base}}({\mathbf{u}})+\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\log\left|\det J_{f^{(\ell)}}({\mathbf{h}}^{(\ell-1)})\right| (2)

where 𝐡(0)=𝐳{\mathbf{h}}^{(0)}={\mathbf{z}}, 𝐡(ℓ)=f(ℓ)​(𝐡(ℓ−1)){\mathbf{h}}^{(\ell)}=f^{(\ell)}({\mathbf{h}}^{(\ell-1)}), and 𝐮=𝐡(L){\mathbf{u}}={\mathbf{h}}^{(L)}.

The main challenge in designing normalizing flows lies in choosing transformations f(ℓ)f^{(\ell)} that are both expressive enough to model complex data distributions and computationally efficient, particularly regarding the calculation of the inverse f−1f^{-1} and the Jacobian determinant detJf\det J_{f}.

A prominent and widely used class is autoregressive flows [39, 50]. These structure the transformation ff such that uiu_{i} depends on zjz_{j} with j<ij<i. This ensures the Jacobian JfJ_{f} is triangular, making its determinant the product of diagonal entries, computable in 𝒪⁡(d)\mathcal{O}(d) time. A common choice for the element-wise transformation is the affine function: zi=αi​ui+βiz_{i}=\alpha_{i}u_{i}+\beta_{i}. In the autoregressive setting, the scale αi>0\alpha_{i}>0 and shift βi\beta_{i} for dimension ii are functions of the preceding dimensions, e.g., αi=αi​(𝐳<i)\alpha_{i}=\alpha_{i}({\mathbf{z}}_{<i}) and βi=βi​(𝐳<i)\beta_{i}=\beta_{i}({\mathbf{z}}_{<i}). If the base variables uiu_{i} are drawn from a standard Gaussian 𝒩⁡(0,1)\mathcal{N}(0,1), this affine transformation implies that each ziz_{i} conditioned on the context 𝐳<i{\mathbf{z}}_{<i} follows a Gaussian distribution 𝒩⁡(zi,μi=βi​(𝐳<i),σi2=αi​(𝐳<i)2)\mathcal{N}(z_{i};\mu_{i}=\beta_{i}({\mathbf{z}}_{<i}),\sigma_{i}^{2}=\alpha_{i}({\mathbf{z}}_{<i})^{2}). To ensure all variables influence each other, multiple autoregressive layers are typically stacked, often with variable permutations between them.

3 Autoregressive Language Modeling in Continuous Latent Space

we use italics for scalars (xtx_{t}), bold for vectors (𝐳t{\mathbf{z}}_{t}), and bold with indices for sequences (𝐱1:T{\mathbf{x}}_{1:T}, 𝐳1:T{\mathbf{z}}_{1:T}).

We propose utilizing the Variational Autoencoder (VAE) framework [38]. The core idea is to map sequences of discrete tokens 𝐱1:T=(x1,…,xT){\mathbf{x}}_{1:T}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{T}) into sequences of continuous latent variables 𝐳1:T=(𝐳1,…,𝐳T){\mathbf{z}}_{1:T}=({\mathbf{z}}_{1},\ldots,{\mathbf{z}}_{T}), where each 𝐳t∈ℝd{\mathbf{z}}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. We then model the joint distribution p(𝐳1:T)p({\mathbf{z}}_{1:T}), the prior, to capture sequential dependencies. This approach aims to preserve the sequential factorization structure familiar from autoregressive models while gaining the benefits of end-to-end differentiability inherent in continuous spaces.

Our model consists of three components (see Figure 1): an encoder q(𝐳1:T|𝐱1:T)q({\mathbf{z}}_{1:T}|{\mathbf{x}}_{1:T}) and decoder p(𝐱1:T|𝐳1:T)p({\mathbf{x}}_{1:T}|{\mathbf{z}}_{1:T}) that map between discrete token sequences and continuous latent sequences, and an autoregressive prior p(𝐳1:T)p({\mathbf{z}}_{1:T}) over the latent space. The model parameters (covering encoder, decoder, and prior) are learned by maximizing the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO) on the data log-likelihood logp(𝐱1:T)\log p({\mathbf{x}}_{1:T}):

ℒ(𝐱1:T)=𝔼𝐳1:T∼q(⋅|𝐱1:T)logp(𝐱1:T|𝐳1:T)⏟decoder+logp(𝐳1:T)⏟prior−logq(𝐳1:T|𝐱1:T)⏟encoder\mathcal{L}({\mathbf{x}}_{1:T})=\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{z}}_{1:T}\sim q(\cdot|{\mathbf{x}}_{1:T})}\underbrace{\log p({\mathbf{x}}_{1:T}|{\mathbf{z}}_{1:T})}_{\text{decoder}}+\underbrace{\log p({\mathbf{z}}_{1:T})}_{\text{prior}}-\underbrace{\log q({\mathbf{z}}_{1:T}|{\mathbf{x}}_{1:T})}_{\text{encoder}} (3)

3.1 The Bridge: Encoder and Decoder

The encoder and decoder facilitate the transition between the discrete data space of tokens and the continuous latent space of vectors 𝐳t{\mathbf{z}}_{t}.

Encoder q(𝐳1:T|𝐱1:T)q({\mathbf{z}}_{1:T}|{\mathbf{x}}_{1:T}).

We use a factorized encoder, q(𝐳1:T|𝐱1:T)=∏t=1Tq(𝐳t|xt)q({\mathbf{z}}_{1:T}|{\mathbf{x}}_{1:T})=\prod_{t=1}^{T}q({\mathbf{z}}_{t}|x_{t}), where each token k∈{1,…,V}k\in\{1,\ldots,V\} is assigned a learnable mean 𝝁k∈ℝd{\bm{\mu}}_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and variance σk2\sigma_{k}^{2} for an isotropic Gaussian: q⁡(𝐳t|xt=k)=𝒩⁡(𝐳t,𝝁k,σk2​𝑰)≡𝒩k​(𝐳t)q({\mathbf{z}}_{t}|x_{t}=k)=\mathcal{N}({\mathbf{z}}_{t};{\bm{\mu}}_{k},\sigma_{k}^{2}{\bm{I}})\equiv\mathcal{N}_{k}({\mathbf{z}}_{t}). Thus, the codebook {𝝁k,σk2}k=1V\{{\bm{\mu}}_{k},\sigma_{k}^{2}\}_{k=1}^{V} maps each token to a Gaussian distribution in latent space.

Decoder p(𝐱1:T|𝐳1:T)p({\mathbf{x}}_{1:T}|{\mathbf{z}}_{1:T}).

The decoder maps each latent vector 𝐳t{\mathbf{z}}_{t} back to a distribution over tokens, with again a factorized structure p(𝐱1:T|𝐳1:T)=∏t=1Tp(xt|𝐳t)p({\mathbf{x}}_{1:T}|{\mathbf{z}}_{1:T})=\prod_{t=1}^{T}p(x_{t}|{\mathbf{z}}_{t}). We reuse the encoder’s Gaussian parameters {𝝁k,σk2}k=1V\{{\bm{\mu}}_{k},\sigma_{k}^{2}\}_{k=1}^{V} for the decoder with a Bayesian posterior parameterization assuming an uniform prior: p⁡(xt=k|𝐳t)=p⁡(xt=k)​q​(𝐳t|xt=k)∑j=1Vp⁡(xt=j)​q​(𝐳t|xt=j)=𝒩k​(𝐳t)∑j=1V𝒩j​(𝐳t)p(x_{t}=k|{\mathbf{z}}_{t})=\frac{p(x_{t}=k)q({\mathbf{z}}_{t}|x_{t}=k)}{\sum_{j=1}^{V}p(x_{t}=j)q({\mathbf{z}}_{t}|x_{t}=j)}=\frac{\mathcal{N}_{k}({\mathbf{z}}_{t})}{\sum_{j=1}^{V}\mathcal{N}_{j}({\mathbf{z}}_{t})}. In other words, the probability of decoding token kk from 𝐳t{\mathbf{z}}_{t} is determined by how likely 𝐳t{\mathbf{z}}_{t} is under the kk-th encoder Gaussian, compared to all other tokens.

3.2 Autoregressive Prior Modeling for p(𝐳1:T)p({\mathbf{z}}_{1:T})

To model the prior p(𝐳1:T)p({\mathbf{z}}_{1:T}) over latent sequences, we use the standard autoregressive factorization: p(𝐳1:T)=∏t=1Tp(𝐳t|𝐳<t)p({\mathbf{z}}_{1:T})=\prod_{t=1}^{T}p({\mathbf{z}}_{t}|{\mathbf{z}}_{<t}), where 𝐳<t=(𝐳1,…,𝐳t−1){\mathbf{z}}_{<t}=({\mathbf{z}}_{1},\ldots,{\mathbf{z}}_{t-1}) is the history. The main task is to define the conditional distribution p⁡(𝐳t|𝐳<t)p({\mathbf{z}}_{t}|{\mathbf{z}}_{<t}). We present two forms of parameterizing conditional p⁡(𝐳t|𝐳<t)p({\mathbf{z}}_{t}|{\mathbf{z}}_{<t}), one with dimension-wise autoregressive factorization Sec. 3.2.1, the other wise token-wise autoregressive factorization Sec. 3.2.2. In each formulation, we use mixture-based probability distribution, and show that we can equivalently convert the mixture probability density into an equivallent invertible normalizing flow layer. And finally show how stacking such flow layers yields an expressive and flexible prior model p(𝐳1:T)p({\mathbf{z}}_{1:T}).

3.2.1 Dimension-wise Autoregressive 11-D Mixture Modeling

We start from decomposing the conditional p⁡(𝐳t|𝐳<t)p({\mathbf{z}}_{t}|{\mathbf{z}}_{<t}) using the chain rule across the dimensions of 𝐳t{\mathbf{z}}_{t}:

p⁡(𝐳t|𝐳<t)=∏i=1dp⁡(zt,i|𝐳<t,𝐳t,<i)p({\mathbf{z}}_{t}|{\mathbf{z}}_{<t})=\prod_{i=1}^{d}p(z_{t,i}|{\mathbf{z}}_{<t},{\mathbf{z}}_{t,<i}) (4)

Here, zt,iz_{t,i} is the ii-th scalar component of 𝐳t{\mathbf{z}}_{t}. 𝐳t,<i=(zt,1,…,zt,i−1){\mathbf{z}}_{t,<i}=(z_{t,1},\ldots,z_{t,i-1}) are its preceding components. We parameterize each scalar conditional density p⁡(zt,i|𝐳<t,𝐳t,<i)p(z_{t,i}|{\mathbf{z}}_{<t},{\mathbf{z}}_{t,<i}) as a mixture of VV 11-dimensional Gaussian distributions. The parameter bundle [𝝅t,i,𝐦t,i,𝝈t,i2]\left[\bm{{\bm{\pi}}}_{t,i},\mathbf{m}_{t,i},\bm{\sigma}_{t,i}^{2}\right] is predicted by a causal Transformer-based model from the context (𝐳<t,𝐳t,<i)({\mathbf{z}}_{<t},{\mathbf{z}}_{t,<i}). The conditional density is then, dropping the subscripts t,it,i here for notational brievity:

p⁡(zt,i|𝐳<t,𝐳t,<i)=∑k=1V𝝅⁡[k]​𝒩​(zt,i,𝐦⁡[k],𝝈2​[k]),[𝝅,𝐦,𝝈2]=Transformer​(𝐳<t,𝐳t,<i)p(z_{t,i}|{\mathbf{z}}_{<t},{\mathbf{z}}_{t,<i})=\sum_{k=1}^{V}{\bm{\pi}}[k]\mathcal{N}(z_{t,i};\mathbf{m}[k],\bm{\sigma}^{2}[k]),\quad\left[{\bm{\pi}},\mathbf{m},\bm{\sigma}^{2}\right]=\text{Transformer}({\mathbf{z}}_{<t},{\mathbf{z}}_{t,<i}) (5)

We denote this 11-D mixture PDF as pmix-​1​(zt,i){p_{\text{mix-}1}}(z_{t,i}). We discuss the connection to the mixture-of-logistics coupling [29] in App. D.

Transforming 11-D Mixture Density to an Invertible Flow.

The conditional 1D mixture density pmix-​1​(⋅){p_{\text{mix-}1}}(\cdot) from Eq. 5 naturally defines an invertible normalizing flow layer. This layer transforms an input zt,iz_{t,i} into ut,iu_{t,i}, such that ut,iu_{t,i} follows a standard normal distribution 𝒩⁡(0,1)\mathcal{N}(0,1). The transformation is given by ut,i=Φ−1​(Fmix-​1​(zt,i,𝐳<t,𝐳t,<i))u_{t,i}=\Phi^{-1}(F_{\text{mix-}1}(z_{t,i};{\mathbf{z}}_{<t},{\mathbf{z}}_{t,<i})), where Fmix-​1F_{\text{mix-}1} is the CDF of pmix-​1{p_{\text{mix-}1}} and Φ−1\Phi^{-1} is the inverse standard normal CDF. This mapping is invertible and its key properties are summarized in Table 1 (see Appendix A for details).

The log absolute Jacobian determinant for this transformation, central to normalizing flows, takes the form log⁡|∂ut,i∂zt,i|=log⁡pmix-​1​(zt,i|𝐳<t,𝐳t,<i)−log⁡𝒩⁡(ut,i,0,1)\log\left|\frac{\partial u_{t,i}}{\partial z_{t,i}}\right|=\log{p_{\text{mix-}1}}(z_{t,i}|{\mathbf{z}}_{<t},{\mathbf{z}}_{t,<i})-\log\mathcal{N}(u_{t,i};0,1). This expresses the log-density of zt,iz_{t,i} under the mixture model as the sum of the log-density of ut,iu_{t,i} under the standard normal and the log-Jacobian:

log⁡pmix-​1​(zt,i|𝐳<t,𝐳t,<i)=log⁡𝒩⁡(ut,i,0,1)+log⁡|∂ut,i∂zt,i|.\log{p_{\text{mix-}1}}(z_{t,i}|{\mathbf{z}}_{<t},{\mathbf{z}}_{t,<i})=\log\mathcal{N}(u_{t,i};0,1)+\log\left|\frac{\partial u_{t,i}}{\partial z_{t,i}}\right|. (6)

In this way, learning the mixture parameters [𝝅,𝐦,𝝈2]\left[{\bm{\pi}},\mathbf{m},\bm{\sigma}^{2}\right] is equivalent to learning a 1D Mixture-CDF flow layer. We summarize this in the following proposition, where we omit the condition 𝐳<t,𝐳t,<i{\mathbf{z}}_{<t},{\mathbf{z}}_{t,<i} for brevity.

3.2.2 Token-wise Autoregressive dd-D Mixture Modeling

Alternatively, p⁡(𝐳t|𝐳<t)p({\mathbf{z}}_{t}|{\mathbf{z}}_{<t}) can be modeled directly as a dd-dimensional distribution. We model p⁡(𝐳t|𝐳<t)p({\mathbf{z}}_{t}|{\mathbf{z}}_{<t}) directly as a dd-dimensional distribution using a mixture of Gaussians with a shared global codebook ΦS={(𝝁k,σk2)}k=1V\Phi_{S}=\{(\bm{\mu}_{k},\sigma_{k}^{2})\}_{k=1}^{V} containing VV Gaussian components. The network only predicts the VV mixture weights 𝝅t​(𝐳<t)\bm{\pi}_{t}({\mathbf{z}}_{<t}) (a VV-dim vector) from the history 𝐳<t{\mathbf{z}}_{<t}:

p⁡(𝐳t|𝐳<t)=∑k=1V𝝅t​(𝐳<t)​[k]​𝒩​(𝐳t,𝝁k,σk2​𝑰),𝝅t​(𝐳<t)=Transformer​(𝐳<t)p({\mathbf{z}}_{t}|{\mathbf{z}}_{<t})=\sum_{k=1}^{V}\bm{\pi}_{t}({\mathbf{z}}_{<t})[k]\mathcal{N}({\mathbf{z}}_{t};\bm{\mu}_{k},\sigma_{k}^{2}{\bm{I}}),\quad\bm{\pi}_{t}({\mathbf{z}}_{<t})=\text{Transformer}({\mathbf{z}}_{<t}) (7)

This approach requires predicting only VV parameters per time step, making it computationally efficient. We denote this dd-dimensional mixture PDF as pmix-​d​(𝐳t|𝐳<t){p_{\text{mix-}d}}({\mathbf{z}}_{t}|{\mathbf{z}}_{<t}).

Connection to Discrete AR Language Models.

This formulation is closely linked to discrete autoregressive language models; see App. F for details.

Transforming dd-D Mixture Density to an Invertible Flow.

The dd-dimensional conditional mixture density pmix-​d{p_{\text{mix-}d}} can also be realized as an invertible normalizing flow layer. Unlike the 1D case, where the CDF and its inverse are available in closed form, a direct CDF-based transformation is not tractable for general dd-dimensional mixtures. Instead, we use a sequential transformation 𝐮=𝐠d​(𝐳,𝐳<t){\mathbf{u}}=\mathbf{g}_{d}({\mathbf{z}};{\mathbf{z}}_{<t}) based on Rosenblatt’s theorem [55], which maps 𝐳∈ℝd{\mathbf{z}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} to 𝐮∈ℝd{\mathbf{u}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} such that 𝐮{\mathbf{u}} follows a standard Gaussian 𝒩⁡(𝟎,𝑰d)\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},{\bm{I}}_{d}). This process, described in Algorithm 1, proceeds dimension by dimension: at each step ii, a 1D Mixture-CDF transform is applied to ziz_{i}, conditioned on the previous components 𝐳<i{\mathbf{z}}_{<i}. The full derivation, including the inverse transformation, is given in Appendix B.

The log absolute Jacobian determinant of this transformation has a form directly analogous to the 1D case (see Appendix B): log⁡|detJ𝐠d​(𝐳)|=log⁡pmix-​d​(𝐳t|𝐳<t)−log⁡𝒩⁡(𝐮,𝟎,𝑰d)\log\left|\det J_{\mathbf{g}_{d}}({\mathbf{z}})\right|=\log{p_{\text{mix-}d}}({\mathbf{z}}_{t}|{\mathbf{z}}_{<t})-\log\mathcal{N}({\mathbf{u}};\mathbf{0},{\bm{I}}_{d}). This relationship, also summarized in Table 1, shows that the log-probability of 𝐳{\mathbf{z}} under the dd-dimensional mixture is given by the change of variables formula:

pmix-​d​(𝐳t|𝐳<t)=log⁡𝒩⁡(𝐮,𝟎,𝑰d)+log⁡|detJ𝐠d​(𝐳)|{p_{\text{mix-}d}}({\mathbf{z}}_{t}|{\mathbf{z}}_{<t})=\log\mathcal{N}({\mathbf{u}};\mathbf{0},{\bm{I}}_{d})+\log\left|\det J_{\mathbf{g}_{d}}({\mathbf{z}})\right| (8)

We summarize this in the following proposition, where we omit the condition 𝐳<t{\mathbf{z}}_{<t} for brevity.

We also provide a proof of the invertibility and differentiability of the proposed Rosenblatt Flow in Proposition 3 in Appendix App. B.

3.3 Stacking Flow Layers for Expressive Priors

To construct a flexible prior p(𝐳1:T)p({\mathbf{z}}_{1:T}) over the latent sequence, we stack multiple invertible flow layers. Each flow f(ℓ)f^{(\ell)} transforms its input 𝐡1:T(ℓ−1){\mathbf{h}}_{1:T}^{(\ell-1)} to output 𝐡1:T(ℓ){\mathbf{h}}_{1:T}^{(\ell)}, starting from 𝐡1:T(0)≜𝐳1:T{\mathbf{h}}_{1:T}^{(0)}\triangleq{\mathbf{z}}_{1:T} and ending with 𝐮1:T≜𝐡1:T(L){\mathbf{u}}_{1:T}\triangleq{\mathbf{h}}_{1:T}^{(L)}, which is modeled by a standard Gaussian base distribution pbase(𝐮1:T)p_{\text{base}}({\mathbf{u}}_{1:T}).

The model is trained by maximizing the ELBO. For a single sample, the per-token objective is:

ℒt≈−log⁡(∑k=1V𝒩k​(𝐳t))+log⁡𝒩⁡(𝐮t,𝟎,𝑰)+∑ℓ=1L[log⁡pmix,t(ℓ)​(𝐡t(ℓ−1)|𝒞t(ℓ))−log⁡𝒩⁡(𝐡t(ℓ),𝟎,𝑰)]\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{t}\approx-\log\left(\sum_{k=1}^{V}\mathcal{N}_{k}({\mathbf{z}}_{t})\right)+\log\mathcal{N}({\mathbf{u}}_{t};\mathbf{0},{\bm{I}})+\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\left[\log p_{\text{mix},t}^{(\ell)}({\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell-1)}|{\mathcal{C}}_{t}^{(\ell)})-\log\mathcal{N}({\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)};\mathbf{0},{\bm{I}})\right] (9)

where the first term applies when using the tied encoder-decoder (Eq. equation 3.1). Here, pmix,t(ℓ)p_{\text{mix},t}^{(\ell)} is the mixture density for the input to layer ℓ\ell, and 𝒞t(ℓ){\mathcal{C}}_{t}^{(\ell)} denotes the conditioning information.

For each flow layer f(ℓ)f^{(\ell)}, the objective is twofold: (a) maximize the log-likelihood of its input under the learned mixture pmix,t(ℓ)p_{\text{mix},t}^{(\ell)}, and (b) encourage the output 𝐡t(ℓ){\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)} to match the standard normal distribution. This is achieved by maximizing log⁡pmix,t(ℓ)​(𝐡t(ℓ−1)|𝒞t(ℓ))−log⁡𝒩⁡(𝐡t(ℓ),𝟎,𝑰)\log p_{\text{mix},t}^{(\ell)}({\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell-1)}|{\mathcal{C}}_{t}^{(\ell)})-\log\mathcal{N}({\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)};\mathbf{0},{\bm{I}}) for each layer and token.

This stacked structure enables the model to incrementally transform the latent variables and capture complex dependencies. Different flow types and autoregressive directions can be combined across layers for greater expressiveness.

Progressive Layer-wise Training

Our stacked normalizing flow prior naturally supports progressive layer-wise training, which simplifies optimization for deep flow models. We start by training the first block of flow layers (e.g., f(1)f^{(1)} to f(k1)f^{(k_{1})}), possibly together with the VAE encoder and decoder, until their ELBO contribution (Eq. equation 9) stabilizes on a validation set. Once converged, we freeze their parameters and add the next block of layers (e.g., f(k1+1)f^{(k_{1}+1)} to f(k2)f^{(k_{2})}), training only the new layers to further transform the fixed output from the previous block. This process repeats, adding and training new layers while keeping earlier ones fixed, until all LL flow layers are trained. Progressive training improves stability, as each new layer incrementally normalizes the representation, and helps the model reach better optima in deep architectures.

4 Experiments

We conduct experiments to evaluate our proposed continuous latent space framework for autoregressive language modeling. The primary objectives are twofold: first, to assess its likelihood performance on standard language modeling benchmarks, and second, to demonstrate the flexible modeling capabilities enabled by the continuous and flow-based formulation.

Datasets and Evaluation.

We evaluate our models on standard language modeling benchmarks, specifically Text8 [47] and OpenWebText [22]. For character-level tasks, we report bits per character (BPC), while for word-level tasks, we use perplexity (PPL) or negative ELBO (NELBO) on the respective test sets, given the VAE-based nature of our model.

Model Configurations.

We conduct our experiments using the GPT2-Small architecture, following the setup in [1, 56, 58]. This model has 12 layers, a hidden size of 768, and 12 attention heads. All conditional distributions within the flow layers are parameterized by Transformers, as described in Sections 3.2.1 and 3.2.2. We primarily explore two model configurations:

  • •

    Mix-1: This variant employs a dimension-wise autoregressive 1-D mixture prior (p⁡(zt,i∣𝐳<t,𝐳t,<i)p(z_{t,i}\mid{\mathbf{z}}_{<t},{\mathbf{z}}_{t,<i}); see Sec. 3.2.1). The model consists of three flow layers with alternating directions (left-to-right and right-to-left), starting from the 𝐳→𝐮{\mathbf{z}}\rightarrow{\mathbf{u}} direction. The number of Transformer layers in each flow is [2,2,8][2,2,8]. Unless otherwise specified in ablation studies, we use V=64V=64 mixture components for OpenWebText and V=27V=27 for Text8. To achieve dimension-wise autoregression, we use the same MLP-based MAF [50] in [41].

  • •

    Mix-d: This variant uses a token-wise autoregressive dd-dimensional mixture prior (p⁡(𝐳t∣𝐳<t)p({\mathbf{z}}_{t}\mid{\mathbf{z}}_{<t}); see Sec. 3.2.2). The model is composed of three flow blocks, trained progressively as outlined in Sec. 3.3. The first flow layer uses Mix-d Mixture-Rosenblatt coupling, with the Gaussian mixture codebook tied to the encoder. The remaining two layers use Mix-1 Mixture-CDF coupling. For OpenWebText, we set V=50257V=50257 in the first flow layer and V=64V=64 in the next two; for Text8, we use V=27V=27 in the first layer and V=2V=2 in the remaining layers.

We use a latent embedding dimension of d=16d=16 for all OpenWebText experiments and d=5d=5 for all Text8 experiments.

Perplexity evaluation

We assess the language modeling capabilities of our approach by training models on three standard benchmarks: Text8, and OpenWebText. For each dataset, we evaluate the NELBO of our trained models on their respective validation or test splits. Specifically, for Text8, we follow the established character-level setup and data splits, typically using fixed-length text chunks for training. For OpenWebText, we train models using the common GPT-2 tokenization and a context length of 1,024 tokens, reserving a portion of the dataset for validation, upon which NELBO is reported. We report results in Table 2.

Importance of Mixture Coupling

We provide empirical evidence for the effectiveness of the mixture coupling layers introduced earlier. Specifically, we compare two model variants on the OpenWebText dataset: (1) a baseline using only affine coupling layers (6 flow blocks, each with a 2-layer causal transformer, totaling 12 transformer layers), and (2) an identical architecture but with Mix-1D (mixture) coupling layers. As shown in Figure Fig. 3, incorporating mixture couplings leads to a substantial improvement in negative ELBO, clearly demonstrating their importance for modeling discrete text data.

Flexible Patch Size: Block-wise Multi-token Generation

Our framework offers greater flexibility in sequence modeling by moving beyond the traditional single-token generation approach. Instead, it processes "patches" of multiple tokens at once, allowing for simultaneous prediction and generation. In contrast, standard discrete autoregressive language models—even those trained with multi-token objectives [21, 42]—still generate tokens strictly one at a time to maintain autoregressive consistency, since generating multiple tokens together breaks their core assumptions. We address this by using a continuous latent space and stacked normalizing flows to capture dependencies within each token patch. First, stacked autoregressive flows with alternating directions (see Figure 1, patch size two) enable later layers to propagate and refine joint information, even if earlier blocks treat tokens as conditionally independent (as shown by the shaded area). Second, intra-patch dependencies are further modeled by mixing or permuting latent embedding dimensions between flow layers (channel mixing, Algorithm 2), allowing information to flow between token positions within a patch. Together, these mechanisms let the model effectively learn intra-patch dependencies. Block-wise generation also changes the computational landscape: it shifts some of the workload from sequence length to model depth (number of flow layers), reducing the effective sequence length. As shown in Figure 7, this can significantly lower the total FLOPs needed to process a sequence (e.g., 1024 tokens) compared to standard transformers, especially with larger patch sizes—all within a generalized autoregressive framework. We also trained a discrete autoregressive language model with a two-token prediction objective and compared its generative perplexity (measured by GPT-2 Large) to our model, conditioning on varying prefix lengths. The results show a large gap, highlighting how standard AR LMs break down when the next-single-token assumption is violated.

Flexible vocabulary size.

A key flexibility of our model is the ability to freely choose the number of mixture components in each stacked autoregressive flow layer, especially when using mixture-based transformations (see Sections 3.2.1 and 3.2.2). This number, denoted as VV in Eq. equation 5 (1D) and Eq. equation 7 (dd-dimensional), serves as an internal "vocabulary" for the flow, and can be set independently for each layer.

This design enables strategies like coarse-to-fine modeling: earlier layers can use fewer components to capture broad structure, while later layers use more to refine details. Importantly, the internal mixture size does not need to match the data’s discrete vocabulary.

Empirically, this flexibility is robust. On Text8, as shown in Fig. 5, the model performs consistently well across a wide range of mixture counts (22 to 2727), even though the dataset’s vocabulary is 2727 characters. On OpenWebText, using 6464 or more mixture components in the mix-1d coupling layers matches the performance of using the full GPT-2 tokenizer size (5025750257). In summary, our framework allows the internal "vocabulary" of mixture components to be tuned for the task, decoupling it from the data’s vocabulary and providing a practical lever for model design and efficiency.

Flexible text editing in continuous space.

Our framework models language in a continuous latent space using stacked autoregressive normalizing flows, enabling us to decode intermediate representations at each flow layer. This provides a unique, step-by-step view of how the model incrementally edits and refines latent states into coherent text—a process that is difficult to realize in discrete token spaces. A key advantage of this approach is its natural support for coarse-to-fine generation: early flow layers make broad, global changes to the latent sequence, while later layers focus on increasingly fine-grained adjustments. We quantify this progression using several metrics, including the mean L2 norm of token embeddings, mean pairwise cosine similarity, Participation Ratio (PR), and centroid movement between layers. Typically, we observe that the mean L2 norm decreases and cosine similarity increases across layers, indicating that representations become more compact and internally coherent. The centroid movement diminishes with depth, reflecting the transition from coarse to fine editing. Alternating flow directions (e.g., left-to-right and right-to-left) further enrich the representations by integrating information from both past and future context. This hierarchical, coarse-to-fine refinement is a direct benefit of operating in a continuous space, where smooth, learnable edits are possible at every stage. For further details and quantitative results, see Appendix G.

Model Ablation

We performed ablation studies on OpenWebText to evaluate key architectural choices (see Figure 3). Adding dimension-wise autoregressive affine flows to a base model yields only minor NELBO improvement. Replacing affine couplings with 1-D mixture-CDF transforms greatly improves NELBO, and using full dd-dimensional Mixture-Rosenblatt flow further boosts performance. Progressive layer-wise training—freezing earlier flow blocks—achieves the best results, demonstrating the benefit of a simple curriculum over flow depth. We also examined the effect of the number of Gaussian components VV in 11-D mixture-CDF couplings on Text8 (Figure 5). We did not use MAF module to isolate the mixture coupling effect. A single component (affine flow) gives high BPC, while all other >1>1 number of mixtures can work well.

5 Conclusion

This work introduced TarFlowLM, a novel framework that recasts language modeling in continuous latent spaces using Transformer-based autoregressive normalizing flows. Our approach achieves strong likelihood performance while enabling significant flexibility, including bi-directional context, block-wise generation, and hierarchical refinement. These findings highlight the potential of continuous latent variable models with mixture-based transformations to advance flexible and expressive sequence generation.

Limitations

While our framework, TarFlowLM, demonstrates strong likelihood performance and notable modeling flexibility, we acknowledge certain limitations inherent to the current instantiation, particularly concerning sampling efficiency. Autoregressive normalizing flows, by their nature, involve a sequential generation process. Each step in the generation depends on the previously generated ones, which can lead to slower sampling speeds compared to models that allow for more parallelized generation, such as some non-autoregressive or diffusion-based approaches.

In this work, our primary focus was on establishing the viability of transformer-based autoregressive flows for flexible language modeling in continuous latent spaces, emphasizing likelihood estimation and the exploration of novel modeling capabilities like block-wise generation and hierarchical refinement. Consequently, a systematic investigation into optimizing sampling speed or exploring advanced sampling techniques (e.g., parallel decoding strategies, distillation) for this class of flow-based language models was beyond the scope of the current paper.

Improving the sampling efficiency of autoregressive flow models for text generation remains an important and active area of research. We consider this a promising direction for future work, which could involve developing specialized architectural modifications, exploring alternative flow parametrizations, or adapting techniques from other generative modeling paradigms to accelerate the sampling process without compromising the expressive power and flexibility demonstrated in this paper.

Broader Impacts

The research presented in this paper, TarFlowLM, introduces a novel framework for language modeling in continuous latent spaces using transformer-based autoregressive normalizing flows. As with many advancements in machine learning and artificial intelligence, particularly in the domain of generative models, this work has the potential for a range of societal impacts, both positive and negative.

Potential Positive Societal Impacts.

The enhanced flexibility offered by our approach—such as bi-directional context modeling, block-wise generation, and hierarchical refinement—could lead to significant positive developments.

  • •

    Improved Creative Tools: Models capable of more nuanced and controllable generation could serve as powerful assistive tools for writers, artists, and designers, helping to brainstorm, draft, and refine creative content. The ability to edit text in a continuous latent space and observe intermediate generation steps might offer new paradigms for human-AI collaboration in creative tasks.

  • •

    Enhanced Controllability in NLP Applications: The flexible architectural components, like adaptable patch sizes and independent mixture component selection per layer, might enable finer-grained control over the generation process. This could be beneficial for applications requiring specific stylistic attributes, content constraints, or conditional generation tasks (e.g., personalized dialogue systems, summarization with specific focuses).

  • •

    Advancements in Fundamental Understanding: By exploring language modeling in continuous latent spaces, this research contributes to a broader understanding of how complex sequential data can be represented and manipulated. Such foundational insights can spur further innovation in machine learning for sequences beyond just text, potentially impacting fields like bioinformatics or time-series analysis.

  • •

    Potential for More Efficient Modeling: While sampling efficiency is noted as a limitation, the architectural flexibility (e.g., block-wise processing potentially reducing effective sequence length for attention mechanisms) hints at avenues for developing more computationally efficient models for certain tasks or sequence lengths, which could make advanced NLP capabilities more accessible.

Potential Negative Societal Impacts and Risks.

Advancements in generative language modeling, including the techniques explored in this paper, also carry inherent risks that warrant careful consideration.

  • •

    Economic Disruption: As generative AI tools become more capable, there is potential for economic disruption in professions that involve content creation or communication. While these tools can also augment human capabilities, the long-term societal adjustments need to be considered.

  • •

    Security Concerns: The potential for generating human-like text could be used in social engineering attacks, to create more convincing phishing emails, or to automate an abusive online presence.

Considerations for Responsible Development.

While this work is primarily foundational, focusing on a novel modeling paradigm, it is crucial for the research community to engage in ongoing discussions about the responsible development and deployment of such technologies. Future research building upon TarFlowLM should ideally incorporate investigations into:

  • •

    Techniques for detecting synthetically generated text from such continuous-space flow models.

  • •

    Methods for identifying and mitigating biases in the learned representations and generated outputs.

  • •

    Developing frameworks for controllable and ethical AI, ensuring that generative capabilities are aligned with human values and safety.

Our aim is to contribute to the open scientific exploration of generative models. We believe that by understanding the capabilities and limitations of new approaches like TarFlowLM, the community is better equipped to foresee potential impacts and work towards harnessing these technologies for societal benefit while mitigating potential harms.

Appendix

Appendix A Details for 11-D Mixture-CDF Flow Layer

This section details the derivation for the 1D Mixture of Gaussians CDF (Cumulative Distribution Function) normalizing flow layer, as introduced in Section 3.2.1 of the main text. The conditional mixture density for a single scalar component zt,iz_{t,i} given its context (𝐳<t,𝐳t,<i)({\mathbf{z}}_{<t},{\mathbf{z}}_{t,<i}) is defined in Eq. equation 5 as:

p⁡(zt,i|𝐳<t,𝐳t,<i)=∑k=1V𝝅⁡[k]​𝒩​(zt,i,𝐦⁡[k],𝝈2​[k])p(z_{t,i}|{\mathbf{z}}_{<t},{\mathbf{z}}_{t,<i})=\sum_{k=1}^{V}{\bm{\pi}}[k]\mathcal{N}(z_{t,i};\mathbf{m}[k],\bm{\sigma}^{2}[k])

where the parameter bundle [𝝅,𝐦,𝝈2]\left[{\bm{\pi}},\mathbf{m},\bm{\sigma}^{2}\right] (containing VV mixture weights, means, and variances respectively) is predicted by a Transformer model from the context (𝐳<t,𝐳t,<i)({\mathbf{z}}_{<t},{\mathbf{z}}_{t,<i}). We denote this 1D mixture probability density function (PDF) as pmix-​1​(zt,i|𝐳<t,𝐳t,<i){p_{\text{mix-}1}}(z_{t,i}|{\mathbf{z}}_{<t},{\mathbf{z}}_{t,<i}). This conditional PDF can be used to construct an invertible transformation suitable for normalizing flows.

The CDF of pmix-​1​(zt,i|𝐳<t,𝐳t,<i){p_{\text{mix-}1}}(z_{t,i}|{\mathbf{z}}_{<t},{\mathbf{z}}_{t,<i}), denoted Fmix-​1​(zt,i,𝐳<t,𝐳t,<i)F_{\text{mix-}1}(z_{t,i};{\mathbf{z}}_{<t},{\mathbf{z}}_{t,<i}), is a weighted sum of the CDFs of the individual Gaussian components:

Fmix-​1​(zt,i,𝐳<t,𝐳t,<i)=∑k=1V𝝅⁡[k]​Φ​(zt,i−𝐦⁡[k]𝝈⁡[k])F_{\text{mix-}1}(z_{t,i};{\mathbf{z}}_{<t},{\mathbf{z}}_{t,<i})=\sum_{k=1}^{V}{\bm{\pi}}[k]\Phi\left(\frac{z_{t,i}-\mathbf{m}[k]}{\bm{\sigma}[k]}\right)

where Φ⁡(⋅)\Phi(\cdot) is the CDF of the standard normal distribution 𝒩⁡(0,1)\mathcal{N}(0,1), and 𝝈⁡[k]=𝝈2​[k]\bm{\sigma}[k]=\sqrt{\bm{\sigma}^{2}[k]} is the standard deviation of the kk-th component. The mixture parameters 𝝅⁡[k],𝐦⁡[k],𝝈⁡[k]{\bm{\pi}}[k],\mathbf{m}[k],\bm{\sigma}[k] are functions of (𝐳<t,𝐳t,<i)({\mathbf{z}}_{<t},{\mathbf{z}}_{t,<i}).

Using the probability integral transform, if a random variable Zt,iZ_{t,i} is drawn from pmix-​1​(Zt,i|𝐳<t,𝐳t,<i){p_{\text{mix-}1}}(Z_{t,i}|{\mathbf{z}}_{<t},{\mathbf{z}}_{t,<i}), then Fmix-​1​(Zt,i,𝐳<t,𝐳t,<i)F_{\text{mix-}1}(Z_{t,i};{\mathbf{z}}_{<t},{\mathbf{z}}_{t,<i}) is uniformly distributed on [0,1][0,1]. To map zt,iz_{t,i} to a variable ut,iu_{t,i} that follows a standard normal distribution 𝒩⁡(0,1)\mathcal{N}(0,1), we compose the mixture CDF with the inverse standard normal CDF, Φ−1​(⋅)\Phi^{-1}(\cdot):

ut,i=Φ−1​(Fmix-​1​(zt,i,𝐳<t,𝐳t,<i))u_{t,i}=\Phi^{-1}(F_{\text{mix-}1}(z_{t,i};{\mathbf{z}}_{<t},{\mathbf{z}}_{t,<i})) (10)

This transformation is invertible. The variable zt,iz_{t,i} can be recovered from ut,iu_{t,i} using zt,i=Fmix-​1−1​(Φ⁡(ut,i),𝐳<t,𝐳t,<i)z_{t,i}=F_{\text{mix-}1}^{-1}(\Phi(u_{t,i});{\mathbf{z}}_{<t},{\mathbf{z}}_{t,<i}), where Fmix-​1−1F_{\text{mix-}1}^{-1} is the inverse CDF (quantile function) of the mixture. Fmix-​1−1F_{\text{mix-}1}^{-1} generally does not have a closed-form expression and may require numerical methods for its evaluation.

For this transformation to serve as a normalizing flow layer, its Jacobian determinant is needed. In this 1D case, this is the absolute value of the derivative ∂ut,i∂zt,i\frac{\partial u_{t,i}}{\partial z_{t,i}}. We compute this using the chain rule. Let ycdf=Fmix-​1​(zt,i,𝐳<t,𝐳t,<i)y_{\text{cdf}}=F_{\text{mix-}1}(z_{t,i};{\mathbf{z}}_{<t},{\mathbf{z}}_{t,<i}). Then ut,i=Φ−1​(ycdf)u_{t,i}=\Phi^{-1}(y_{\text{cdf}}), and

∂ut,i∂zt,i=d​Φ−1​(ycdf)d​ycdf|ycdf=Fmix-​1​(zt,i,𝐳<t,𝐳t,<i)⋅∂Fmix-​1​(zt,i,𝐳<t,𝐳t,<i)∂zt,i\frac{\partial u_{t,i}}{\partial z_{t,i}}=\frac{d\Phi^{-1}(y_{\text{cdf}})}{dy_{\text{cdf}}}\Bigg|_{y_{\text{cdf}}=F_{\text{mix-}1}(z_{t,i};{\mathbf{z}}_{<t},{\mathbf{z}}_{t,<i})}\cdot\frac{\partial F_{\text{mix-}1}(z_{t,i};{\mathbf{z}}_{<t},{\mathbf{z}}_{t,<i})}{\partial z_{t,i}}

We evaluate each term:

  1. 1.

    The derivative of the inverse standard normal CDF, d​Φ−1​(ycdf)d​ycdf\frac{d\Phi^{-1}(y_{\text{cdf}})}{dy_{\text{cdf}}}: If ut,i=Φ−1​(ycdf)u_{t,i}=\Phi^{-1}(y_{\text{cdf}}), then ycdf=Φ⁡(ut,i)y_{\text{cdf}}=\Phi(u_{t,i}). Differentiating ycdf=Φ⁡(ut,i)y_{\text{cdf}}=\Phi(u_{t,i}) with respect to ut,iu_{t,i} yields d​ycdfd​ut,i=𝒩⁡(ut,i,0,1)\frac{dy_{\text{cdf}}}{du_{t,i}}=\mathcal{N}(u_{t,i};0,1), where 𝒩⁡(ut,i,0,1)\mathcal{N}(u_{t,i};0,1) is the PDF of the standard normal distribution. Therefore, d​ut,id​ycdf=d​Φ−1​(ycdf)d​ycdf=1𝒩⁡(ut,i,0,1)\frac{du_{t,i}}{dy_{\text{cdf}}}=\frac{d\Phi^{-1}(y_{\text{cdf}})}{dy_{\text{cdf}}}=\frac{1}{\mathcal{N}(u_{t,i};0,1)}.

  2. 2.

    The derivative of the mixture CDF with respect to zt,iz_{t,i}, ∂Fmix-​1​(zt,i,𝐳<t,𝐳t,<i)∂zt,i\frac{\partial F_{\text{mix-}1}(z_{t,i};{\mathbf{z}}_{<t},{\mathbf{z}}_{t,<i})}{\partial z_{t,i}}:

    ∂Fmix-​1​(zt,i,𝐳<t,𝐳t,<i)∂zt,i\displaystyle\frac{\partial F_{\text{mix-}1}(z_{t,i};{\mathbf{z}}_{<t},{\mathbf{z}}_{t,<i})}{\partial z_{t,i}} =∂∂zt,i​∑k=1V𝝅⁡[k]​Φ​(zt,i−𝐦⁡[k]𝝈⁡[k])\displaystyle=\frac{\partial}{\partial z_{t,i}}\sum_{k=1}^{V}{\bm{\pi}}[k]\Phi\left(\frac{z_{t,i}-\mathbf{m}[k]}{\bm{\sigma}[k]}\right)
    =∑k=1V𝝅⁡[k]​𝒩​(zt,i−𝐦⁡[k]𝝈⁡[k],0,1)⋅1𝝈⁡[k]\displaystyle=\sum_{k=1}^{V}{\bm{\pi}}[k]\mathcal{N}\left(\frac{z_{t,i}-\mathbf{m}[k]}{\bm{\sigma}[k]};0,1\right)\cdot\frac{1}{\bm{\sigma}[k]}

    Recognizing that 1𝝈⁡[k]​𝒩​(zt,i−𝐦⁡[k]𝝈⁡[k],0,1)\frac{1}{\bm{\sigma}[k]}\mathcal{N}\left(\frac{z_{t,i}-\mathbf{m}[k]}{\bm{\sigma}[k]};0,1\right) is the PDF 𝒩⁡(zt,i,𝐦⁡[k],𝝈2​[k])\mathcal{N}(z_{t,i};\mathbf{m}[k],\bm{\sigma}^{2}[k]), the sum becomes:

    ∂Fmix-​1​(zt,i,𝐳<t,𝐳t,<i)∂zt,i=∑k=1V𝝅⁡[k]​𝒩​(zt,i,𝐦⁡[k],𝝈2​[k])=pmix-​1​(zt,i|𝐳<t,𝐳t,<i)\frac{\partial F_{\text{mix-}1}(z_{t,i};{\mathbf{z}}_{<t},{\mathbf{z}}_{t,<i})}{\partial z_{t,i}}=\sum_{k=1}^{V}{\bm{\pi}}[k]\mathcal{N}(z_{t,i};\mathbf{m}[k],\bm{\sigma}^{2}[k])={p_{\text{mix-}1}}(z_{t,i}|{\mathbf{z}}_{<t},{\mathbf{z}}_{t,<i})

    Thus, the derivative of the mixture CDF is its PDF.

Combining these results, the derivative of the transformation is:

∂ut,i∂zt,i=pmix-​1​(zt,i|𝐳<t,𝐳t,<i)𝒩⁡(ut,i,0,1)\frac{\partial u_{t,i}}{\partial z_{t,i}}=\frac{{p_{\text{mix-}1}}(z_{t,i}|{\mathbf{z}}_{<t},{\mathbf{z}}_{t,<i})}{\mathcal{N}(u_{t,i};0,1)}

The log absolute Jacobian determinant is therefore:

log⁡|∂ut,i∂zt,i|=log⁡pmix-​1​(zt,i|𝐳<t,𝐳t,<i)−log⁡𝒩⁡(ut,i,0,1)\log\left|\frac{\partial u_{t,i}}{\partial z_{t,i}}\right|=\log{p_{\text{mix-}1}}(z_{t,i}|{\mathbf{z}}_{<t},{\mathbf{z}}_{t,<i})-\log\mathcal{N}(u_{t,i};0,1) (11)

This equation relates the log-density of zt,iz_{t,i} under the mixture model pmix-​1{p_{\text{mix-}1}} to the log-density of ut,iu_{t,i} under the standard normal base distribution and the log-Jacobian term. Rearranging Eq. equation 11 according to the change of variables formula (log⁡p⁡(z)=log⁡p⁡(u)+log⁡|detJf|\log p(z)=\log p(u)+\log|\det J_{f}|):

log⁡pmix-​1​(zt,i|𝐳<t,𝐳t,<i)=log⁡𝒩⁡(ut,i,0,1)+log⁡|∂ut,i∂zt,i|\log{p_{\text{mix-}1}}(z_{t,i}|{\mathbf{z}}_{<t},{\mathbf{z}}_{t,<i})=\log\mathcal{N}(u_{t,i};0,1)+\log\left|\frac{\partial u_{t,i}}{\partial z_{t,i}}\right|

This confirms that learning the mixture parameters [𝝅,𝐦,𝝈2]\left[{\bm{\pi}},\mathbf{m},\bm{\sigma}^{2}\right] is equivalent to learning this 1D Mixture-CDF flow layer.

When such a transformation is used as a layer ℓ\ell in a stack of flows, zt,iz_{t,i} corresponds to the ii-th scalar component of the input to this layer, ht,i(ℓ−1)h_{t,i}^{(\ell-1)}. The output ut,iu_{t,i} corresponds to the ii-th scalar component ht,i(ℓ)h_{t,i}^{(\ell)}. The parameters for the mixture density pmix-​1​(ht,i(ℓ−1)|condt,i(ℓ)){p_{\text{mix-}1}}(h_{t,i}^{(\ell-1)}|\text{cond}_{t,i}^{(\ell)}) for layer ℓ\ell are determined by a neural network conditioned on condt,i(ℓ)\text{cond}_{t,i}^{(\ell)}, which is the layer-specific conditioning information. The term log⁡pmix-​1​(ht,i(ℓ−1)|condt,i(ℓ))\log{p_{\text{mix-}1}}(h_{t,i}^{(\ell-1)}|\text{cond}_{t,i}^{(\ell)}) in the log-determinant calculation (Eq. equation 11, adapted for layer ℓ\ell) represents the log-probability of the layer’s input under the specific 1D mixture model implemented by that layer.

A.1 Proof of Proposition 1

Proposition 1.

Let pmix−1​(z)=∑k=1Vπk​𝒩​(z,mk,σk2)p_{\mathrm{mix-1}}(z)=\sum_{k=1}^{V}\pi_{k}\mathcal{N}(z;m_{k},\sigma_{k}^{2}) be a 1D MoG probability density function (PDF), and let Fmix−1​(z)F_{\mathrm{mix-1}}(z) be its corresponding cumulative distribution function (CDF). The transformation f:ℝ→ℝf:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} defined by u=f⁡(z)=Φ−1​(Fmix−1​(z))u=f(z)=\Phi^{-1}(F_{\mathrm{mix-1}}(z)), where Φ\Phi is the standard normal CDF, is an exact normalizing flow between the density pmix−1​(z)p_{\mathrm{mix-1}}(z) and the standard normal density 𝒩⁡(u,0,1)\mathcal{N}(u;0,1).

Proof.

The proof demonstrates the equivalence from both forward and inverse directions. A key property is that Fmix−1​(z)F_{\mathrm{mix-1}}(z) is strictly increasing, since its derivative, Fmix−1′​(z)=pmix−1​(z)F^{\prime}_{\mathrm{mix-1}}(z)=p_{\mathrm{mix-1}}(z), is a sum of strictly positive Gaussian densities and is therefore strictly positive. Thus, Fmix−1F_{\mathrm{mix-1}} is a bijection from ℝ\mathbb{R} to (0,1)(0,1).

Forward Direction (Z→UZ\to U). Assume a random variable Z∼pmix−1​(z)Z\sim p_{\mathrm{mix-1}}(z). We show that the transformed variable U=f⁡(Z)U=f(Z) follows a standard normal distribution by computing its CDF:

P⁡(U≤u)\displaystyle P(U\leq u) =P⁡(Φ−1​(Fmix−1​(Z))≤u)\displaystyle=P\bigl(\Phi^{-1}(F_{\mathrm{mix-1}}(Z))\leq u\bigr)
=P⁡(Fmix−1​(Z)≤Φ⁡(u))\displaystyle=P\bigl(F_{\mathrm{mix-1}}(Z)\leq\Phi(u)\bigr) (since ​Φ​ is strictly increasing)\displaystyle\text{(since }\Phi\text{ is strictly increasing)}
=Fmix−1​(Fmix−1−1​(Φ⁡(u)))\displaystyle=F_{\mathrm{mix-1}}\bigl(F_{\mathrm{mix-1}}^{-1}(\Phi(u))\bigr) (by definition, ​P​(Z≤z′)=Fmix−1​(z′)​)\displaystyle\text{(by definition, }P(Z\leq z^{\prime})=F_{\mathrm{mix-1}}(z^{\prime})\text{)}
=Φ⁡(u).\displaystyle=\Phi(u).

The CDF of UU is Φ⁡(u)\Phi(u), which is the CDF of the standard normal distribution. Hence, U∼𝒩⁡(0,1)U\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1).

Inverse Direction (U→ZU\to Z). Assume a random variable U∼𝒩⁡(0,1)U\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1). We show that Z=f−1​(U)=Fmix−1−1​(Φ⁡(U))Z=f^{-1}(U)=F_{\mathrm{mix-1}}^{-1}(\Phi(U)) is distributed according to pmix−1​(z)p_{\mathrm{mix-1}}(z) by computing its CDF:

P⁡(Z≤z)\displaystyle P(Z\leq z) =P⁡(Fmix−1−1​(Φ⁡(U))≤z)\displaystyle=P\bigl(F_{\mathrm{mix-1}}^{-1}(\Phi(U))\leq z\bigr)
=P⁡(Φ⁡(U)≤Fmix−1​(z))\displaystyle=P\bigl(\Phi(U)\leq F_{\mathrm{mix-1}}(z)\bigr) (since ​Fmix−1​ is strictly increasing).\displaystyle\text{(since }F_{\mathrm{mix-1}}\text{ is strictly increasing)}.

By the probability integral transform, the random variable Φ⁡(U)\Phi(U) is uniformly distributed on [0,1][0,1]. Therefore, P⁡(Φ⁡(U)≤v)=vP\bigl(\Phi(U)\leq v\bigr)=v for any v∈[0,1]v\in[0,1]. Since Fmix−1​(z)∈(0,1)F_{\mathrm{mix-1}}(z)\in(0,1), we have:

P⁡(Z≤z)=Fmix−1​(z).P(Z\leq z)=F_{\mathrm{mix-1}}(z).

The CDF of ZZ is Fmix−1​(z)F_{\mathrm{mix-1}}(z). Differentiating with respect to zz yields the PDF of ZZ as pZ​(z)=dd​z​Fmix−1​(z)=pmix−1​(z)p_{Z}(z)=\frac{d}{dz}F_{\mathrm{mix-1}}(z)=p_{\mathrm{mix-1}}(z), which completes the proof. ∎

Appendix B Details for dd-D Mixture-Rosenblatt Flow Layer

We use 𝒞{\mathcal{C}} to denote the conditioning context variable. A dd-dimensional conditional mixture density, such as pmix​(𝐳|𝒞)=∑k=1Vπk​(𝒞)​𝒩​(𝐳,𝐦k​(𝒞),sk2​(𝒞)​𝑰d)p_{\text{mix}}({\mathbf{z}}|{\mathcal{C}})=\sum_{k=1}^{V}\pi_{k}({\mathcal{C}})\mathcal{N}({\mathbf{z}};\mathbf{m}_{k}({\mathcal{C}}),s_{k}^{2}({\mathcal{C}}){\bm{I}}_{d}), can be realized as an exact and invertible normalizing flow layer. This construction is used for modeling complex conditional distributions within the flow framework. For example, it can represent the prior’s conditional distribution p⁡(𝐳t|𝐳<t)p({\mathbf{z}}_{t}|{\mathbf{z}}_{<t}) as defined in Eq. equation 7, or a general conditional density pmix,t(ℓ)​(𝐡t(ℓ−1)|condt(ℓ))p_{\text{mix},t}^{(\ell)}({\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell-1)}|\text{cond}_{t}^{(\ell)}) for an intermediate layer ℓ\ell in a stack of flows (see Section 3.3).

In this description, 𝐳∈ℝd{\mathbf{z}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} denotes the input variable to this flow layer. If this layer is the first transformation applied to a latent variable 𝐳t{\mathbf{z}}_{t} from the VAE, then 𝐳{\mathbf{z}} corresponds to 𝐳t{\mathbf{z}}_{t} (which is also 𝐡t(0){\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(0)} in the notation of stacked flows). If it is an intermediate layer ℓ\ell in the stack, 𝐳{\mathbf{z}} corresponds to 𝐡t(ℓ−1){\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell-1)}. The term 𝒞{\mathcal{C}} represents the conditioning information, such as 𝐳<t{\mathbf{z}}_{<t} for the prior, or a layer-specific context condt(ℓ)\text{cond}_{t}^{(\ell)}. The parameters 𝐦k\mathbf{m}_{k} and sk2s_{k}^{2} of the Gaussian components can either be predicted based on 𝒞{\mathcal{C}}, or, as in Eq. equation 7, they can be part of a shared codebook (e.g., {𝝁k,σk2}k=1V\{\bm{\mu}_{k},\sigma_{k}^{2}\}_{k=1}^{V}) where only the mixture weights πk​(𝒞)\pi_{k}({\mathcal{C}}) are predicted.

The goal is to define an invertible transformation 𝐠d:ℝd→ℝd\mathbf{g}_{d}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}, denoted 𝐮=𝐠d​(𝐳,𝒞){\mathbf{u}}=\mathbf{g}_{d}({\mathbf{z}};{\mathcal{C}}), such that the output variable 𝐮∈ℝd{\mathbf{u}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} follows a standard dd-dimensional Gaussian distribution, i.e., 𝐮∼𝒩⁡(𝟎,𝑰d){\mathbf{u}}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},{\bm{I}}_{d}). This transformation is constructed by processing the components of 𝐳=(z1,…,zd){\mathbf{z}}=(z_{1},\ldots,z_{d}) sequentially, from i=1i=1 to dd, using a method related to the Rosenblatt transformation. The forward pass is detailed in Algorithm 1.

Forward Transformation 𝐳↦𝐮{\mathbf{z}}\mapsto{\mathbf{u}}: The transformation from 𝐳{\mathbf{z}} to 𝐮{\mathbf{u}} is built sequentially, processing one component at a time. At each step ii, uiu_{i} is computed from ziz_{i} using 𝒞{\mathcal{C}} and the previously processed components 𝐳<i=(z1,…,zi−1){\mathbf{z}}_{<i}=(z_{1},\ldots,z_{i-1}). Mixture component weights are maintained and updated throughout this process.

The procedure begins with initialization: for the first component z1z_{1}, the initial mixture weights are set by the parameters of pmix​(𝐳|𝒞)p_{\text{mix}}({\mathbf{z}}|{\mathcal{C}}),

αk(1)​(𝒞)=πk​(𝒞)for ​k=1,…,V.\alpha_{k}^{(1)}({\mathcal{C}})=\pi_{k}({\mathcal{C}})\quad\text{for }k=1,\ldots,V. (12)

For each dimension i=1,…,di=1,\ldots,d, the following steps are performed: The forward transformation proceeds as follows. For each dimension i=1,…,di=1,\ldots,d:

Conditional Density of ziz_{i}. The conditional probability density of ziz_{i} given 𝒞{\mathcal{C}} and 𝐳<i{\mathbf{z}}_{<i} is a 1D mixture of Gaussians, denoted pmix,i​(zi|𝒞,𝐳<i)p_{\text{mix},i}(z_{i}|{\mathcal{C}},{\mathbf{z}}_{<i}). This is computed by marginalizing over the mixture components using the current weights αk(i)\alpha_{k}^{(i)}:

pmix,i​(zi|𝒞,𝐳<i)=∑k=1Vαk(i)​(𝒞,𝐳<i)​𝒩​(zi,mk,i​(𝒞),sk2​(𝒞))p_{\text{mix},i}(z_{i}|{\mathcal{C}},{\mathbf{z}}_{<i})=\sum_{k=1}^{V}\alpha_{k}^{(i)}({\mathcal{C}},{\mathbf{z}}_{<i})\mathcal{N}(z_{i};m_{k,i}({\mathcal{C}}),s_{k}^{2}({\mathcal{C}})) (13)

Here, mk,i​(𝒞)m_{k,i}({\mathcal{C}}) is the ii-th element of the mean vector 𝐦k​(𝒞)\mathbf{m}_{k}({\mathcal{C}}) for component kk, and sk2​(𝒞)s_{k}^{2}({\mathcal{C}}) is the (isotropic) variance for component kk. By construction, pmix,i​(zi|𝒞,𝐳<i)p_{\text{mix},i}(z_{i}|{\mathcal{C}},{\mathbf{z}}_{<i}) is equivalent to p⁡(zi|𝒞,𝐳<i)p(z_{i}|{\mathcal{C}},{\mathbf{z}}_{<i}).

Conditional CDF of ziz_{i}. The corresponding 1D conditional cumulative distribution function (CDF) for ziz_{i} is

Fi​(zi|𝒞,𝐳<i)=∫−∞zipmix,i​(ξ|𝒞,𝐳<i)​𝑑ξ=∑k=1Vαk(i)​(𝒞,𝐳<i)​Φ​(zi−mk,i​(𝒞)sk​(𝒞))F_{i}(z_{i}|{\mathcal{C}},{\mathbf{z}}_{<i})=\int_{-\infty}^{z_{i}}p_{\text{mix},i}(\xi|{\mathcal{C}},{\mathbf{z}}_{<i})d\xi=\sum_{k=1}^{V}\alpha_{k}^{(i)}({\mathcal{C}},{\mathbf{z}}_{<i})\Phi\left(\frac{z_{i}-m_{k,i}({\mathcal{C}})}{s_{k}({\mathcal{C}})}\right) (14)

where Φ⁡(⋅)\Phi(\cdot) is the CDF of the standard normal distribution and sk​(𝒞)=sk2​(𝒞)s_{k}({\mathcal{C}})=\sqrt{s_{k}^{2}({\mathcal{C}})}.

Transformation to uiu_{i}. The ii-th component uiu_{i} of the transformed variable 𝐮{\mathbf{u}} is obtained by applying the probability integral transform to ziz_{i} using FiF_{i}, followed by the inverse CDF of the standard normal:

ui=Φ−1​(Fi​(zi|𝒞,𝐳<i))u_{i}=\Phi^{-1}(F_{i}(z_{i}|{\mathcal{C}},{\mathbf{z}}_{<i})) (15)

If ziz_{i} is drawn from pmix,i​(zi|𝒞,𝐳<i)p_{\text{mix},i}(z_{i}|{\mathcal{C}},{\mathbf{z}}_{<i}), then Fi​(zi|𝒞,𝐳<i)F_{i}(z_{i}|{\mathcal{C}},{\mathbf{z}}_{<i}) is uniformly distributed on [0,1][0,1], and thus uiu_{i} is standard normal. The sequential conditioning ensures that u1,…,udu_{1},\ldots,u_{d} are mutually independent and standard normally distributed.

Update Mixture Weights (if i<di<d). After processing ziz_{i} and obtaining uiu_{i}, if ii is not the last dimension, the mixture weights for the next dimension, αk(i+1)\alpha_{k}^{(i+1)}, are updated using Bayes’ rule to incorporate the information from ziz_{i}:

αk(i+1)​(𝒞,𝐳≤i)\displaystyle\alpha_{k}^{(i+1)}({\mathcal{C}},{\mathbf{z}}_{\leq i}) =p⁡(component=k|𝒞,𝐳≤i)\displaystyle=p(\text{component}=k|{\mathcal{C}},{\mathbf{z}}_{\leq i})
=p⁡(zi|component=k,𝒞,𝐳<i)⋅p⁡(component=k|𝒞,𝐳<i)p⁡(zi|𝒞,𝐳<i)\displaystyle=\frac{p(z_{i}|\text{component}=k,{\mathcal{C}},{\mathbf{z}}_{<i})\cdot p(\text{component}=k|{\mathcal{C}},{\mathbf{z}}_{<i})}{p(z_{i}|{\mathcal{C}},{\mathbf{z}}_{<i})}
=𝒩⁡(zi,mk,i​(𝒞),sk2​(𝒞))⋅αk(i)​(𝒞,𝐳<i)pmix,i​(zi|𝒞,𝐳<i)\displaystyle=\frac{\mathcal{N}(z_{i};m_{k,i}({\mathcal{C}}),s_{k}^{2}({\mathcal{C}}))\cdot\alpha_{k}^{(i)}({\mathcal{C}},{\mathbf{z}}_{<i})}{p_{\text{mix},i}(z_{i}|{\mathcal{C}},{\mathbf{z}}_{<i})} (16)

where 𝐳≤i=(z1,…,zi){\mathbf{z}}_{\leq i}=(z_{1},\ldots,z_{i}). These updated weights are then used for the next dimension.

Inverse Transformation 𝐮↦𝐳{\mathbf{u}}\mapsto{\mathbf{z}}: The transformation 𝐠d\mathbf{g}_{d} is invertible. To compute the inverse, 𝐳=𝐠d−1​(𝐮,𝒞){\mathbf{z}}=\mathbf{g}_{d}^{-1}({\mathbf{u}};{\mathcal{C}}), we proceed as follows, iterating from i=1i=1 to dd:

Initialization (for i=1i=1): Set the initial mixture weights αk(1)​(𝒞)\alpha_{k}^{(1)}({\mathcal{C}}) as in Eq. equation 12.

Sequential Inversion (for i=1,…,di=1,\ldots,d): For each dimension ii, given uiu_{i} and the current weights αk(i)​(𝒞,𝐳<i)\alpha_{k}^{(i)}({\mathcal{C}},{\mathbf{z}}_{<i}) (where 𝐳<i{\mathbf{z}}_{<i} have been determined in previous steps), solve for ziz_{i} by finding the value that satisfies

Fi​(zi|𝒞,𝐳<i)=Φ⁡(ui)F_{i}(z_{i}|{\mathcal{C}},{\mathbf{z}}_{<i})=\Phi(u_{i}) (17)

where FiF_{i} is defined in Eq. equation 14. Since FiF_{i} is a strictly monotonic function (as the CDF of a continuous distribution with positive density), a unique solution for ziz_{i} exists. This inversion typically requires a numerical 1D root-finding algorithm.

After determining ziz_{i}, if i<di<d, update the mixture weights to αk(i+1)​(𝒞,𝐳≤i)\alpha_{k}^{(i+1)}({\mathcal{C}},{\mathbf{z}}_{\leq i}) using Eq. equation 16, now with the newly found ziz_{i}. This process is repeated sequentially for each dimension until all components of 𝐳{\mathbf{z}} are recovered.

Jacobian Determinant: The Jacobian matrix J𝐠d​(𝐳)J_{\mathbf{g}_{d}}({\mathbf{z}}) of the forward transformation 𝐮=𝐠d​(𝐳,𝒞){\mathbf{u}}=\mathbf{g}_{d}({\mathbf{z}};{\mathcal{C}}) has entries (J𝐠d)ℓ​i=∂uℓ∂zi(J_{\mathbf{g}_{d}})_{\ell i}=\frac{\partial u_{\ell}}{\partial z_{i}}. Due to the sequential construction, where uℓu_{\ell} depends only on z1,…,zℓz_{1},\ldots,z_{\ell} (and 𝒞{\mathcal{C}}), the Jacobian matrix is lower-triangular. Its determinant is the product of its diagonal entries: detJ𝐠d​(𝐳)=∏i=1d∂ui∂zi\det J_{\mathbf{g}_{d}}({\mathbf{z}})=\prod_{i=1}^{d}\frac{\partial u_{i}}{\partial z_{i}}.

To find ∂ui∂zi\frac{\partial u_{i}}{\partial z_{i}}, we differentiate Eq. equation 15, or its form Φ⁡(ui)=Fi​(zi|𝒞,𝐳<i)\Phi(u_{i})=F_{i}(z_{i}|{\mathcal{C}},{\mathbf{z}}_{<i}). Differentiating both sides with respect to ziz_{i} (treating 𝒞{\mathcal{C}} and 𝐳<i{\mathbf{z}}_{<i} as constant for this partial derivative):

∂(Φ⁡(ui))∂zi=∂(Fi​(zi|𝒞,𝐳<i))∂zi\frac{\partial(\Phi(u_{i}))}{\partial z_{i}}=\frac{\partial(F_{i}(z_{i}|{\mathcal{C}},{\mathbf{z}}_{<i}))}{\partial z_{i}} (18)

Using the chain rule on the left side yields ϕ⁡(ui)​∂ui∂zi\phi(u_{i})\frac{\partial u_{i}}{\partial z_{i}}, where ϕ⁡(⋅)\phi(\cdot) is the PDF of 𝒩⁡(0,1)\mathcal{N}(0,1). The right side is the derivative of a CDF with respect to its variable, which is its PDF: ∂Fi∂zi=pmix,i​(zi|𝒞,𝐳<i)\frac{\partial F_{i}}{\partial z_{i}}=p_{\text{mix},i}(z_{i}|{\mathcal{C}},{\mathbf{z}}_{<i}). Thus,

ϕ⁡(ui)​∂ui∂zi=pmix,i​(zi|𝒞,𝐳<i)\phi(u_{i})\frac{\partial u_{i}}{\partial z_{i}}=p_{\text{mix},i}(z_{i}|{\mathcal{C}},{\mathbf{z}}_{<i}) (19)

Since ϕ⁡(ui)>0\phi(u_{i})>0, we can write:

∂ui∂zi=pmix,i​(zi|𝒞,𝐳<i)ϕ⁡(ui)\frac{\partial u_{i}}{\partial z_{i}}=\frac{p_{\text{mix},i}(z_{i}|{\mathcal{C}},{\mathbf{z}}_{<i})}{\phi(u_{i})} (20)

The log absolute Jacobian determinant is then:

log⁡|detJ𝐠d​(𝐳)|\displaystyle\log\left|\det J_{\mathbf{g}_{d}}({\mathbf{z}})\right| =∑i=1dlog⁡|∂ui∂zi|\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{d}\log\left|\frac{\partial u_{i}}{\partial z_{i}}\right|
=∑i=1d(log⁡pmix,i​(zi|𝒞,𝐳<i)−log⁡ϕ⁡(ui))\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{d}\left(\log p_{\text{mix},i}(z_{i}|{\mathcal{C}},{\mathbf{z}}_{<i})-\log\phi(u_{i})\right) (21)

By the chain rule of probability, the log-density of the input variable 𝐳{\mathbf{z}} under the conditional mixture pmix​(𝐳|𝒞)p_{\text{mix}}({\mathbf{z}}|{\mathcal{C}}) is:

log⁡pmix​(𝐳|𝒞)=log⁡(∏i=1dp⁡(zi|𝒞,𝐳<i))=∑i=1dlog⁡p⁡(zi|𝒞,𝐳<i)\log p_{\text{mix}}({\mathbf{z}}|{\mathcal{C}})=\log\left(\prod_{i=1}^{d}p(z_{i}|{\mathcal{C}},{\mathbf{z}}_{<i})\right)=\sum_{i=1}^{d}\log p(z_{i}|{\mathcal{C}},{\mathbf{z}}_{<i}) (22)

In our construction, p⁡(zi|𝒞,𝐳<i)p(z_{i}|{\mathcal{C}},{\mathbf{z}}_{<i}) is precisely pmix,i​(zi|𝒞,𝐳<i)p_{\text{mix},i}(z_{i}|{\mathcal{C}},{\mathbf{z}}_{<i}) from Eq. equation 13. So, ∑i=1dlog⁡pmix,i​(zi|𝒞,𝐳<i)=log⁡pmix​(𝐳|𝒞)\sum_{i=1}^{d}\log p_{\text{mix},i}(z_{i}|{\mathcal{C}},{\mathbf{z}}_{<i})=\log p_{\text{mix}}({\mathbf{z}}|{\mathcal{C}}). The log-density of the transformed variable 𝐮{\mathbf{u}} under the standard dd-dimensional Gaussian base distribution pbase​(𝐮)=𝒩⁡(𝐮,𝟎,𝑰d)p_{\text{base}}({\mathbf{u}})=\mathcal{N}({\mathbf{u}};\mathbf{0},{\bm{I}}_{d}) is log⁡pbase​(𝐮)=∑i=1dlog⁡𝒩⁡(ui,0,1)=∑i=1dlog⁡ϕ⁡(ui)\log p_{\text{base}}({\mathbf{u}})=\sum_{i=1}^{d}\log\mathcal{N}(u_{i};0,1)=\sum_{i=1}^{d}\log\phi(u_{i}). Substituting these into Eq. equation 21, we arrive at the expression for the log-determinant in normalizing flows:

log⁡|detJ𝐠d​(𝐳)|=log⁡pmix​(𝐳|𝒞)−log⁡𝒩⁡(𝐮,𝟎,𝑰d)\log\left|\det J_{\mathbf{g}_{d}}({\mathbf{z}})\right|=\log p_{\text{mix}}({\mathbf{z}}|{\mathcal{C}})-\log\mathcal{N}({\mathbf{u}};\mathbf{0},{\bm{I}}_{d}) (23)

This confirms that the sequential transformation 𝐠d\mathbf{g}_{d} correctly implements the desired conditional mixture density pmix​(𝐳|𝒞)p_{\text{mix}}({\mathbf{z}}|{\mathcal{C}}) as a normalizing flow layer. When such a layer is used, for example as layer ft(ℓ)f_{t}^{(\ell)} in a stack, it transforms an input 𝐡t(ℓ−1){\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell-1)} (which plays the role of 𝐳{\mathbf{z}} in this derivation) to an output 𝐡t(ℓ){\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)} (which plays the role of 𝐮{\mathbf{u}}). The parameters defining the mixture (initial weights πk​(condt(ℓ))\pi_{k}(\text{cond}_{t}^{(\ell)}), means 𝐦k​(condt(ℓ))\mathbf{m}_{k}(\text{cond}_{t}^{(\ell)}), and variances sk2​(condt(ℓ))s_{k}^{2}(\text{cond}_{t}^{(\ell)})) are predicted by a neural network based on a conditioning context condt(ℓ)\text{cond}_{t}^{(\ell)}.

B.1 Proof of Proposition 2

Here we provide formal proofs for the normalizing flow layers based on the Mixture of Gaussians (MoG) CDF, as described in Appendices A and B. We establish that these transformations are exact, invertible, and correctly model the target mixture densities.

The core of the dd-dimensional Mixture-Rosenblatt flow lies in sequentially computing the true conditional probability distribution p⁡(zi|𝐳<i)p(z_{i}|{\mathbf{z}}_{<i}) for each dimension. The following lemma formally derives this distribution and shows that it takes the form of a 1D Mixture of Gaussians, which is analytically tractable.

Lemma 1 (Conditional Distribution of an Isotropic MoG).

Let 𝐳∈ℝd{\mathbf{z}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} be a random vector whose probability density function is a mixture of VV isotropic Gaussians:

p⁡(𝐳)=∑k=1Vπk​𝒩​(𝐳,𝐦k,σk2​𝐈d),p({\mathbf{z}})=\sum_{k=1}^{V}\pi_{k}\mathcal{N}({\mathbf{z}};\mathbf{m}_{k},\sigma_{k}^{2}\mathbf{I}_{d}),

where ∑kπk=1\sum_{k}\pi_{k}=1, πk>0\pi_{k}>0. Then for any dimension i∈{1,…,d}i\in\{1,\dots,d\}, the true conditional probability density of its component ziz_{i} given the preceding components 𝐳<i=(z1,…,zi−1){\mathbf{z}}_{<i}=(z_{1},\dots,z_{i-1}) is also a 1D Mixture of Gaussians, given by:

p⁡(zi|𝐳<i)=∑k=1Vαk(i)​(𝐳<i)​𝒩​(zi,mk,i,σk2),p(z_{i}|{\mathbf{z}}_{<i})=\sum_{k=1}^{V}\alpha_{k}^{(i)}({\mathbf{z}}_{<i})\mathcal{N}(z_{i};m_{k,i},\sigma_{k}^{2}),

where mk,im_{k,i} is the ii-th element of 𝐦k\mathbf{m}_{k}, and the mixture weights αk(i)​(𝐳<i)\alpha_{k}^{(i)}({\mathbf{z}}_{<i}) are the posterior probabilities of component membership given 𝐳<i{\mathbf{z}}_{<i}:

αk(i)​(𝐳<i)≜P⁡(K=k|𝐳<i)=πk​𝒩​(𝐳<i,𝐦k,<i,σk2​𝐈i−1)∑j=1Vπj​𝒩​(𝐳<i,𝐦j,<i,σj2​𝐈i−1).\alpha_{k}^{(i)}({\mathbf{z}}_{<i})\triangleq P(K=k|{\mathbf{z}}_{<i})=\frac{\pi_{k}\mathcal{N}({\mathbf{z}}_{<i};\mathbf{m}_{k,<i},\sigma_{k}^{2}\mathbf{I}_{i-1})}{\sum_{j=1}^{V}\pi_{j}\mathcal{N}({\mathbf{z}}_{<i};\mathbf{m}_{j,<i},\sigma_{j}^{2}\mathbf{I}_{i-1})}.

(For the base case i=1i=1, 𝐳<1{\mathbf{z}}_{<1} is empty and αk(1)=πk\alpha_{k}^{(1)}=\pi_{k}).

Proof.

We derive the conditional distribution p⁡(zi|𝐳<i)p(z_{i}|{\mathbf{z}}_{<i}) by introducing a latent categorical variable K∈{1,…,V}K\in\{1,\dots,V\} that indicates which Gaussian component 𝐳{\mathbf{z}} is drawn from. The hierarchical model is:

  1. 1.

    Sample a component index K=kK=k with probability P⁡(K=k)=πkP(K=k)=\pi_{k}.

  2. 2.

    Sample 𝐳{\mathbf{z}} from the chosen component: p⁡(𝐳|K=k)=𝒩⁡(𝐳,𝐦k,σk2​𝐈d)p({\mathbf{z}}|K=k)=\mathcal{N}({\mathbf{z}};\mathbf{m}_{k},\sigma_{k}^{2}\mathbf{I}_{d}).

The target conditional density can be found by marginalizing over this latent variable using the law of total probability:

p⁡(zi|𝐳<i)=∑k=1Vp⁡(zi|𝐳<i,K=k)​P​(K=k|𝐳<i).p(z_{i}|{\mathbf{z}}_{<i})=\sum_{k=1}^{V}p(z_{i}|{\mathbf{z}}_{<i},K=k)P(K=k|{\mathbf{z}}_{<i}). (24)

We now analyze the two terms in the summation separately.

1. The Component Density: p⁡(zi|𝐳<i,K=k)p(z_{i}|{\mathbf{z}}_{<i},K=k). This term is the conditional density of ziz_{i} given 𝐳<i{\mathbf{z}}_{<i}, under the condition that we know the sample originates from component kk. For a given component kk, 𝐳{\mathbf{z}} follows a single multivariate Gaussian distribution 𝒩⁡(𝐦k,σk2​𝐈d)\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{m}_{k},\sigma_{k}^{2}\mathbf{I}_{d}). The covariance matrix σk2​𝐈d\sigma_{k}^{2}\mathbf{I}_{d} is diagonal, which implies that all dimensions of 𝐳{\mathbf{z}} are mutually independent *when conditioned on K=kK=k*. Therefore, the value of ziz_{i} is independent of the preceding values 𝐳<i{\mathbf{z}}_{<i}:

p⁡(zi|𝐳<i,K=k)=p⁡(zi|K=k).p(z_{i}|{\mathbf{z}}_{<i},K=k)=p(z_{i}|K=k).

The distribution p⁡(zi|K=k)p(z_{i}|K=k) is the ii-th marginal of the multivariate Gaussian 𝒩⁡(𝐳,𝐦k,σk2​𝐈d)\mathcal{N}({\mathbf{z}};\mathbf{m}_{k},\sigma_{k}^{2}\mathbf{I}_{d}), which is a 1D Gaussian:

p⁡(zi|K=k)=𝒩⁡(zi,mk,i,σk2).p(z_{i}|K=k)=\mathcal{N}(z_{i};m_{k,i},\sigma_{k}^{2}).

2. The Mixture Weights: P⁡(K=k|𝐳<i)P(K=k|{\mathbf{z}}_{<i}). This term represents the posterior probability of being in component kk after observing the first i−1i-1 dimensions. We denote this by αk(i)​(𝐳<i)\alpha_{k}^{(i)}({\mathbf{z}}_{<i}) and compute it using Bayes’ rule:

P⁡(K=k|𝐳<i)=p⁡(𝐳<i|K=k)​P​(K=k)p⁡(𝐳<i)=p⁡(𝐳<i|K=k)​P​(K=k)∑j=1Vp⁡(𝐳<i|K=j)​P​(K=j).P(K=k|{\mathbf{z}}_{<i})=\frac{p({\mathbf{z}}_{<i}|K=k)P(K=k)}{p({\mathbf{z}}_{<i})}=\frac{p({\mathbf{z}}_{<i}|K=k)P(K=k)}{\sum_{j=1}^{V}p({\mathbf{z}}_{<i}|K=j)P(K=j)}.

The required terms are:

  • •

    P⁡(K=k)=πkP(K=k)=\pi_{k} (the prior probability of selecting component kk).

  • •

    p⁡(𝐳<i|K=k)p({\mathbf{z}}_{<i}|K=k) is the marginal density of the first i−1i-1 dimensions of the kk-th Gaussian. Due to the isotropic structure, this is 𝒩⁡(𝐳<i,𝐦k,<i,σk2​𝐈i−1)\mathcal{N}({\mathbf{z}}_{<i};\mathbf{m}_{k,<i},\sigma_{k}^{2}\mathbf{I}_{i-1}), where 𝐦k,<i\mathbf{m}_{k,<i} contains the first i−1i-1 elements of 𝐦k\mathbf{m}_{k}.

Substituting these into the formula gives the expression for the weights as stated in the lemma.

Conclusion. Substituting the derived component density and mixture weights back into Eq. equation 24, we obtain:

p⁡(zi|𝐳<i)=∑k=1Vαk(i)​(𝐳<i)⏟Mixture Weight⋅𝒩⁡(zi,mk,i,σk2)⏟1D Gaussian Component.p(z_{i}|{\mathbf{z}}_{<i})=\sum_{k=1}^{V}\underbrace{\alpha_{k}^{(i)}({\mathbf{z}}_{<i})}_{\text{Mixture Weight}}\cdot\underbrace{\mathcal{N}(z_{i};m_{k,i},\sigma_{k}^{2})}_{\text{1D Gaussian Component}}.

This confirms that the true conditional distribution is a 1D Mixture of Gaussians with analytically computable parameters. ∎

With the analytical form of the conditional distribution established, we can now state and prove the proposition for the dd-dimensional flow in a more direct manner.

Proposition 2.

Let pmix​(𝐳)=∑k=1Vπk​𝒩​(𝐳,𝐦k,σk2​𝐈d)p_{\mathrm{mix}}({\mathbf{z}})=\sum_{k=1}^{V}\pi_{k}\mathcal{N}({\mathbf{z}};\mathbf{m}_{k},\sigma_{k}^{2}\mathbf{I}_{d}) be a dd-dimensional isotropic MoG PDF. Let the transformation 𝐠:ℝd→ℝd\mathbf{g}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d} be defined by the sequential application for i=1,…,di=1,\dots,d:

ui=gi​(𝐳)=Φ−1​(Fi​(zi|𝐳<i)),u_{i}=g_{i}({\mathbf{z}})=\Phi^{-1}\bigl(F_{i}(z_{i}|{\mathbf{z}}_{<i})\bigr),

where Fi​(zi|𝐳<i)F_{i}(z_{i}|{\mathbf{z}}_{<i}) is the cumulative distribution function (CDF) of the 1D MoG conditional density p⁡(zi|𝐳<i)p(z_{i}|{\mathbf{z}}_{<i}) as derived in Lemma 1. This transformation is an exact normalizing flow between pmix​(𝐳)p_{\mathrm{mix}}({\mathbf{z}}) and the standard dd-dimensional normal distribution 𝒩⁡(𝐮,𝟎,𝐈d)\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{u};\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}_{d}).

Proof.

The proof relies on the chain rule of probability, pmix​(𝐳)=∏i=1dp⁡(zi|𝐳<i)p_{\mathrm{mix}}({\mathbf{z}})=\prod_{i=1}^{d}p(z_{i}|{\mathbf{z}}_{<i}), and the result of Lemma 1.

Forward Direction (𝐙→𝐔\mathbf{Z}\to\mathbf{U}). Assume a random vector 𝐙∼pmix​(𝐳)\mathbf{Z}\sim p_{\mathrm{mix}}({\mathbf{z}}). We show by induction that the components of the transformed vector 𝐔=𝐠⁡(𝐙)\mathbf{U}=\mathbf{g}(\mathbf{Z}) are independent and identically distributed as 𝒩⁡(0,1)\mathcal{N}(0,1). By Lemma 1, Fi​(Zi|𝐙<i)F_{i}(Z_{i}|\mathbf{Z}_{<i}) is the true conditional CDF of ZiZ_{i}. By the conditional probability integral transform, the random variable Wi=Fi​(Zi|𝐙<i)W_{i}=F_{i}(Z_{i}|\mathbf{Z}_{<i}) is uniformly distributed on [0,1][0,1] and is independent of the conditioning random vector 𝐙<i\mathbf{Z}_{<i}. Consequently, Ui=Φ−1​(Wi)U_{i}=\Phi^{-1}(W_{i}) is distributed as 𝒩⁡(0,1)\mathcal{N}(0,1) and is also independent of 𝐙<i\mathbf{Z}_{<i}. Since (U1,…,Ui−1)(U_{1},\dots,U_{i-1}) is an invertible function of 𝐙<i\mathbf{Z}_{<i}, UiU_{i} is also independent of (U1,…,Ui−1)(U_{1},\dots,U_{i-1}). By induction, all components of 𝐔\mathbf{U} are i.i.d. 𝒩⁡(0,1)\mathcal{N}(0,1), so 𝐔∼𝒩⁡(𝟎,𝐈d)\mathbf{U}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}_{d}).

Inverse Direction (𝐔→𝐙\mathbf{U}\to\mathbf{Z}). Assume a random vector 𝐔∼𝒩⁡(𝟎,𝐈d)\mathbf{U}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}_{d}). The inverse transformation 𝐙=𝐠−1​(𝐔)\mathbf{Z}=\mathbf{g}^{-1}(\mathbf{U}) is computed by sequentially solving Fi​(Zi|𝐙<i)=Φ⁡(Ui)F_{i}(Z_{i}|\mathbf{Z}_{<i})=\Phi(U_{i}) for ZiZ_{i}. This procedure is equivalent to ancestral sampling from the factorized distribution: for each i=1,…,di=1,\dots,d, one samples ZiZ_{i} from the true conditional distribution p⁡(zi|𝐙<i)p(z_{i}|\mathbf{Z}_{<i}) via inverse transform sampling. The joint density of the resulting vector 𝐙\mathbf{Z} is therefore ∏i=1dp⁡(zi|𝐳<i)=pmix​(𝐳)\prod_{i=1}^{d}p(z_{i}|{\mathbf{z}}_{<i})=p_{\mathrm{mix}}({\mathbf{z}}).

Jacobian Determinant. The Jacobian of 𝐠\mathbf{g} is lower-triangular, as uiu_{i} depends only on 𝐳≤i{\mathbf{z}}_{\leq i}. Its determinant is the product of the diagonal entries ∂ui∂zi\frac{\partial u_{i}}{\partial z_{i}}. Treating 𝐳<i{\mathbf{z}}_{<i} as constant, we have:

∂ui∂zi=dd​zi​Φ−1​(Fi​(zi|𝐳<i))=Fi′​(zi|𝐳<i)ϕ⁡(ui)=p⁡(zi|𝐳<i)ϕ⁡(ui),\frac{\partial u_{i}}{\partial z_{i}}=\frac{d}{dz_{i}}\Phi^{-1}\bigl(F_{i}(z_{i}|{\mathbf{z}}_{<i})\bigr)=\frac{F_{i}^{\prime}(z_{i}|{\mathbf{z}}_{<i})}{\phi(u_{i})}=\frac{p(z_{i}|{\mathbf{z}}_{<i})}{\phi(u_{i})},

where ϕ\phi is the standard normal PDF and we used the fact that the derivative of a CDF is its PDF. The log-determinant is:

log⁡|detJ𝐠​(𝐳)|=∑i=1dlog⁡|∂ui∂zi|=∑i=1d(log⁡p⁡(zi|𝐳<i)−log⁡ϕ⁡(ui)).\log|\det J_{\mathbf{g}}({\mathbf{z}})|=\sum_{i=1}^{d}\log\left|\frac{\partial u_{i}}{\partial z_{i}}\right|=\sum_{i=1}^{d}\left(\log p(z_{i}|{\mathbf{z}}_{<i})-\log\phi(u_{i})\right).

Using the chain rule of probability for the first term and the definition of the multivariate normal for the second term, this simplifies to:

log⁡|detJ𝐠​(𝐳)|=log⁡pmix​(𝐳)−log⁡𝒩⁡(𝐮,𝟎,𝐈d).\log|\det J_{\mathbf{g}}({\mathbf{z}})|=\log p_{\mathrm{mix}}({\mathbf{z}})-\log\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{u};\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}_{d}).

This confirms that the change of variables formula is satisfied exactly. The recursive Bayesian update algorithm described in Appendix B is the practical implementation of the analytical derivation in Lemma 1. ∎

B.2 Proof of Proposition 3

We now prove that the multidimensional transformation is a global diffeomorphism, which is a stronger condition than mere invertibility and differentiability, ensuring the transformation is smooth and stable.

Proposition 3.

Let pmix​(𝐳)=∑k=1Vπk​𝒩​(𝐳,𝐦k,σk2​𝐈d)p_{\mathrm{mix}}({\mathbf{z}})=\sum_{k=1}^{V}\pi_{k}\mathcal{N}({\mathbf{z}};\mathbf{m}_{k},\sigma_{k}^{2}\mathbf{I}_{d}) be a dd-dimensional MoG PDF. The Rosenblatt transformation 𝐠:ℝd→ℝd\mathbf{g}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}, defined sequentially by

ui=gi​(𝐳)=Φ−1​(Fi​(zi|𝐳<i))for ​i=1,…,d,u_{i}=g_{i}({\mathbf{z}})=\Phi^{-1}\bigl(F_{i}(z_{i}|{\mathbf{z}}_{<i})\bigr)\quad\text{for }i=1,\dots,d,

where FiF_{i} is the CDF of the true conditional density p⁡(zi|𝐳<i)p(z_{i}|{\mathbf{z}}_{<i}), is a global C∞C^{\infty}-diffeomorphism.

Proof.

Our proof strategy is to first show that 𝐠\mathbf{g} is a local diffeomorphism everywhere on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} and then establish that it is also a global bijection. These two properties together imply that 𝐠\mathbf{g} is a global diffeomorphism.

Local Diffeomorphism. A map is a local C∞C^{\infty}-diffeomorphism at a point if it is smooth (C∞C^{\infty}) in a neighborhood of that point and its Jacobian determinant is non-zero at that point.

(a) Smoothness of 𝐠\mathbf{g}: The map 𝐠\mathbf{g} is smooth if each component function ui=gi​(𝐳)u_{i}=g_{i}({\mathbf{z}}) is smooth. The function gi=Φ−1∘Fig_{i}=\Phi^{-1}\circ F_{i} is a composition of functions. The conditional density p⁡(zi|𝐳<i)p(z_{i}|{\mathbf{z}}_{<i}) is a ratio of marginal densities of the MoG. Since marginals of a MoG are themselves finite sums of Gaussian PDFs, they are smooth functions. As the denominator is strictly positive, p⁡(zi|𝐳<i)p(z_{i}|{\mathbf{z}}_{<i}) is a smooth function of all its arguments, (zi,𝐳<i)(z_{i},{\mathbf{z}}_{<i}). By differentiation under the integral sign, its CDF Fi​(zi|𝐳<i)F_{i}(z_{i}|{\mathbf{z}}_{<i}) is also smooth. Since Φ−1\Phi^{-1} is smooth on its domain, the composition gig_{i} is smooth. Thus, the overall map 𝐠\mathbf{g} is smooth on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}.

(b) Non-Vanishing Jacobian Determinant: The Jacobian matrix J𝐠​(𝐳)J_{\mathbf{g}}({\mathbf{z}}) is lower-triangular due to the sequential construction of 𝐠\mathbf{g}. Its determinant is the product of its diagonal entries:

detJ𝐠​(𝐳)=∏i=1d∂ui∂zi=∏i=1dp⁡(zi|𝐳<i)ϕ⁡(ui).\det J_{\mathbf{g}}({\mathbf{z}})=\prod_{i=1}^{d}\frac{\partial u_{i}}{\partial z_{i}}=\prod_{i=1}^{d}\frac{p(z_{i}|{\mathbf{z}}_{<i})}{\phi(u_{i})}.

Since both the conditional density p⁡(zi|𝐳<i)p(z_{i}|{\mathbf{z}}_{<i}) and the standard normal PDF ϕ⁡(ui)\phi(u_{i}) are strictly positive everywhere, each diagonal term is strictly positive. Consequently, detJ𝐠​(𝐳)>0\det J_{\mathbf{g}}({\mathbf{z}})>0 for all 𝐳∈ℝd{\mathbf{z}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}.

By the Inverse Function Theorem, since 𝐠\mathbf{g} is smooth and its Jacobian determinant is non-zero everywhere, 𝐠\mathbf{g} is a local C∞C^{\infty}-diffeomorphism at every point in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}.

Global Bijectivity. We show that 𝐠\mathbf{g} is a bijection by constructing a unique inverse 𝐳=𝐠−1​(𝐮){\mathbf{z}}=\mathbf{g}^{-1}(\mathbf{u}) for any 𝐮∈ℝd\mathbf{u}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. The inverse is found by solving Φ⁡(ui)=Fi​(zi|𝐳<i)\Phi(u_{i})=F_{i}(z_{i}|{\mathbf{z}}_{<i}) for each ziz_{i} sequentially. For any i=1,…,di=1,\dots,d, and for any fixed, previously determined context 𝐳<i{\mathbf{z}}_{<i}, the function Fi(⋅|𝐳<i)F_{i}(\cdot|{\mathbf{z}}_{<i}) is a strictly increasing bijection from ℝ→(0,1)\mathbb{R}\to(0,1). Thus, a unique solution zi=Fi−1​(Φ⁡(ui)|𝐳<i)z_{i}=F_{i}^{-1}(\Phi(u_{i})|{\mathbf{z}}_{<i}) exists at each step. This inductive construction yields a unique 𝐳{\mathbf{z}} for any 𝐮\mathbf{u}, proving that 𝐠\mathbf{g} is a global bijection.

A map that is a local diffeomorphism at every point and is also a global bijection is a global diffeomorphism. Having established both properties for 𝐠\mathbf{g}, we conclude that it is a global C∞C^{\infty}-diffeomorphism from ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} to ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. This confirms that the transformation is smooth, globally invertible with a smooth inverse, and possesses a well-defined, non-zero Jacobian determinant, making it a robust and theoretically sound building block for normalizing flows. ∎

Appendix C Detailed Derivation of a Flow Layer’s Learning Objective

This appendix provides a detailed, step-by-step derivation of the learning objective for a single layer within the normalizing flow prior. The aim is to elucidate how the optimization process shapes the behavior of each transformation in the flow.

We consider a generic invertible transformation ft(ℓ):ℝd→ℝdf_{t}^{(\ell)}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d} representing a single layer ℓ\ell at time step tt in the flow. Let 𝐱=𝐡t(ℓ−1){\mathbf{x}}={\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell-1)} be the input to this layer and 𝐲=𝐡t(ℓ){\mathbf{y}}={\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)} be its output, so 𝐲=ft(ℓ)​(𝐱,condt(ℓ)){\mathbf{y}}=f_{t}^{(\ell)}({\mathbf{x}};\text{cond}_{t}^{(\ell)}). The function ft(ℓ)f_{t}^{(\ell)} is parameterized, and its parameters (and thus its behavior) are learned based on a conditioning context condt(ℓ)\text{cond}_{t}^{(\ell)}. For brevity in the derivations that follow, we will often drop the explicit indices (t,ℓ)(t,\ell) and the conditioning context, writing f⁡(𝐱)f({\mathbf{x}}), pmodel​(𝐱)p_{\text{model}}({\mathbf{x}}), etc., with the understanding that these are specific to a layer and its context.

The Log-Determinant of the Jacobian

The change of variables formula relates the probability density of 𝐱{\mathbf{x}} to the probability density of 𝐲{\mathbf{y}}:

pX​(𝐱)=pY​(f⁡(𝐱))​|detJf​(𝐱)|p_{X}({\mathbf{x}})=p_{Y}(f({\mathbf{x}}))\left|\det J_{f}({\mathbf{x}})\right| (25)

where pXp_{X} is the density of 𝐱{\mathbf{x}}, pYp_{Y} is the density of 𝐲{\mathbf{y}}, and Jf​(𝐱)J_{f}({\mathbf{x}}) is the Jacobian matrix of ff evaluated at 𝐱{\mathbf{x}}.

Normalizing flow layers like those discussed in Sections 3.2.1 and 3.2.2 (e.g., Mixture-of-CDFs or transformations based on dd-dimensional mixtures) are constructed such that they define a conditional model density for their input. Let pmodel​(𝐱|cond)p_{\text{model}}({\mathbf{x}}|\text{cond}) be this parameterized density that the layer learns for its input 𝐱{\mathbf{x}}. The transformation ff is designed such that if 𝐱{\mathbf{x}} were drawn from pmodel​(𝐱|cond)p_{\text{model}}({\mathbf{x}}|\text{cond}), its output 𝐲=f⁡(𝐱){\mathbf{y}}=f({\mathbf{x}}) would be drawn from a simpler, fixed target density, ptarget​(𝐲)p_{\text{target}}({\mathbf{y}}) (typically a standard Gaussian). Substituting pX​(𝐱)=pmodel​(𝐱|cond)p_{X}({\mathbf{x}})=p_{\text{model}}({\mathbf{x}}|\text{cond}) and pY​(𝐲)=ptarget​(𝐲)p_{Y}({\mathbf{y}})=p_{\text{target}}({\mathbf{y}}) into Eq. equation 25, we get:

pmodel​(𝐱|cond)=ptarget​(f⁡(𝐱))​|detJf​(𝐱)|p_{\text{model}}({\mathbf{x}}|\text{cond})=p_{\text{target}}(f({\mathbf{x}}))\left|\det J_{f}({\mathbf{x}})\right| (26)

Rearranging and taking the logarithm gives the expression for the log absolute Jacobian determinant:

log⁡|detJf​(𝐱)|=log⁡pmodel​(𝐱|cond)−log⁡ptarget​(f⁡(𝐱))\log\left|\det J_{f}({\mathbf{x}})\right|=\log p_{\text{model}}({\mathbf{x}}|\text{cond})-\log p_{\text{target}}(f({\mathbf{x}})) (27)

This equation matches the form of  equation 9 in the main text.
