It shows that the log-determinant term, crucial for computing the density of 𝐳1:T{\mathbf{z}}_{1:T}, is composed of the log-likelihood of the input 𝐱{\mathbf{x}} under the layer’s learned model pmodelp_{\text{model}} and the log-likelihood of the output 𝐲=f⁡(𝐱){\mathbf{y}}=f({\mathbf{x}}) under the fixed target density ptargetp_{\text{target}}.

The Expected Log-Jacobian in the ELBO

The parameters of the entire model, including those defining pmodel​(𝐱|cond)p_{\text{model}}({\mathbf{x}}|\text{cond}) for each layer, are learned by maximizing the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO), as shown in Eq. equation 3. The ELBO includes the term 𝔼𝐳1:T∼q(⋅|𝐱1:T)[logp(𝐳1:T)]\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{z}}_{1:T}\sim q(\cdot|{\mathbf{x}}_{1:T})}[\log p({\mathbf{z}}_{1:T})]. The log-prior logp(𝐳1:T)\log p({\mathbf{z}}_{1:T}) is given by a sum of log-base-density terms and log-determinant terms from each layer:

logp(𝐳1:T)=∑t=1T(logpbase(𝐮t)+∑ℓ=1Llog|detJft(ℓ)(𝐡t(ℓ−1))|)\log p({\mathbf{z}}_{1:T})=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left(\log p_{\text{base}}({\mathbf{u}}_{t})+\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\log\left|\det J_{f_{t}^{(\ell)}}({\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell-1)})\right|\right) (28)

Let qin​(𝐱)q_{\text{in}}({\mathbf{x}}) denote the actual distribution of the input 𝐱=𝐡t(ℓ−1){\mathbf{x}}={\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell-1)} to a specific layer f≡ft(ℓ)f\equiv f_{t}^{(\ell)}. This distribution qin​(𝐱)q_{\text{in}}({\mathbf{x}}) is induced by the input data 𝐱1:T{\mathbf{x}}_{1:T}, the encoder q(𝐳1:T|𝐱1:T)q({\mathbf{z}}_{1:T}|{\mathbf{x}}_{1:T}), and all preceding flow transformations f(1),…,f(ℓ−1)f^{(1)},\ldots,f^{(\ell-1)}. The ELBO maximization objective, with respect to the contribution of this layer’s Jacobian to the prior, involves maximizing:

𝒥layer=𝔼qin​(𝐱)​[log⁡|detJf​(𝐱)|]\mathcal{J}_{\text{layer}}=\mathbb{E}_{q_{\text{in}}({\mathbf{x}})}\left[\log\left|\det J_{f}({\mathbf{x}})\right|\right] (29)

Substituting Eq. equation 27:

𝒥layer\displaystyle\mathcal{J}_{\text{layer}} =𝔼qin​(𝐱)​[log⁡pmodel​(𝐱|cond)−log⁡ptarget​(f⁡(𝐱))]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{q_{\text{in}}({\mathbf{x}})}\left[\log p_{\text{model}}({\mathbf{x}}|\text{cond})-\log p_{\text{target}}(f({\mathbf{x}}))\right] (30)
=𝔼qin​(𝐱)​[log⁡pmodel​(𝐱|cond)]−𝔼qin​(𝐱)​[log⁡ptarget​(f⁡(𝐱))]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{q_{\text{in}}({\mathbf{x}})}\left[\log p_{\text{model}}({\mathbf{x}}|\text{cond})\right]-\mathbb{E}_{q_{\text{in}}({\mathbf{x}})}\left[\log p_{\text{target}}(f({\mathbf{x}}))\right] (31)

Let qout​(𝐲)q_{\text{out}}({\mathbf{y}}) be the actual distribution of the output 𝐲=f⁡(𝐱){\mathbf{y}}=f({\mathbf{x}}) when 𝐱∼qin​(𝐱){\mathbf{x}}\sim q_{\text{in}}({\mathbf{x}}). The second term in Eq. equation 31 can be rewritten using this definition:

𝔼qin​(𝐱)​[log⁡ptarget​(f⁡(𝐱))]=𝔼qout​(𝐲)​[log⁡ptarget​(𝐲)]\mathbb{E}_{q_{\text{in}}({\mathbf{x}})}\left[\log p_{\text{target}}(f({\mathbf{x}}))\right]=\mathbb{E}_{q_{\text{out}}({\mathbf{y}})}\left[\log p_{\text{target}}({\mathbf{y}})\right] (32)

So, Eq. equation 31 becomes:

𝒥layer=𝔼qin​(𝐱)​[log⁡pmodel​(𝐱|cond)]−𝔼qout​(𝐲)​[log⁡ptarget​(𝐲)]\mathcal{J}_{\text{layer}}=\mathbb{E}_{q_{\text{in}}({\mathbf{x}})}\left[\log p_{\text{model}}({\mathbf{x}}|\text{cond})\right]-\mathbb{E}_{q_{\text{out}}({\mathbf{y}})}\left[\log p_{\text{target}}({\mathbf{y}})\right] (33)
Relating to KL Divergence and Differential Entropy

We use the definitions of differential entropy H⁡(q)H(q) and Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence KL(q∥p)\mathrm{KL}(q\|p):

H⁡(q)\displaystyle H(q) =−𝔼q⁡(𝐳)[logq(𝐳)]=−∫q(𝐳)logq(𝐳)d𝐳\displaystyle=-\mathbb{E}_{q({\mathbf{z}})}[\log q({\mathbf{z}})]=-\int q({\mathbf{z}})\log q({\mathbf{z}})d{\mathbf{z}} (34)
KL(q∥p)\displaystyle\mathrm{KL}(q\|p) =𝔼q⁡(𝐳)​[log⁡q⁡(𝐳)p⁡(𝐳)]=∫q⁡(𝐳)​log⁡q⁡(𝐳)p⁡(𝐳)​𝑑𝐳\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{q({\mathbf{z}})}\left[\log\frac{q({\mathbf{z}})}{p({\mathbf{z}})}\right]=\int q({\mathbf{z}})\log\frac{q({\mathbf{z}})}{p({\mathbf{z}})}d{\mathbf{z}} (35)

From the definition of KL divergence, we have KL(q∥p)=𝔼q⁡(𝐳)[logq(𝐳)]−𝔼q⁡(𝐳)[logp(𝐳)]=−H(q)−𝔼q⁡(𝐳)[logp(𝐳)]\mathrm{KL}(q\|p)=\mathbb{E}_{q({\mathbf{z}})}[\log q({\mathbf{z}})]-\mathbb{E}_{q({\mathbf{z}})}[\log p({\mathbf{z}})]=-H(q)-\mathbb{E}_{q({\mathbf{z}})}[\log p({\mathbf{z}})]. Rearranging this gives a useful identity for an expected log-likelihood term:

𝔼q⁡(𝐳)[logp(𝐳)]=−H(q)−KL(q∥p)\mathbb{E}_{q({\mathbf{z}})}[\log p({\mathbf{z}})]=-H(q)-\mathrm{KL}(q\|p) (36)

Applying Eq. equation 36 to the two terms in Eq. equation 33:

𝔼qin​(𝐱)​[log⁡pmodel​(𝐱|cond)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{q_{\text{in}}({\mathbf{x}})}\left[\log p_{\text{model}}({\mathbf{x}}|\text{cond})\right] =−H(qin)−KL(qin∥pmodel)\displaystyle=-H(q_{\text{in}})-\mathrm{KL}(q_{\text{in}}\|p_{\text{model}}) (37)
𝔼qout​(𝐲)​[log⁡ptarget​(𝐲)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{q_{\text{out}}({\mathbf{y}})}\left[\log p_{\text{target}}({\mathbf{y}})\right] =−H(qout)−KL(qout∥ptarget)\displaystyle=-H(q_{\text{out}})-\mathrm{KL}(q_{\text{out}}\|p_{\text{target}}) (38)

Substituting these back into the expression for 𝒥layer\mathcal{J}_{\text{layer}}:

𝒥layer\displaystyle\mathcal{J}_{\text{layer}} =[−H(qin)−KL(qin∥pmodel)]−[−H(qout)−KL(qout∥ptarget)]\displaystyle=\left[-H(q_{\text{in}})-\mathrm{KL}(q_{\text{in}}\|p_{\text{model}})\right]-\left[-H(q_{\text{out}})-\mathrm{KL}(q_{\text{out}}\|p_{\text{target}})\right] (39)
=H(qout)−H(qin)−KL(qin∥pmodel)+KL(qout∥ptarget)\displaystyle=H(q_{\text{out}})-H(q_{\text{in}})-\mathrm{KL}(q_{\text{in}}\|p_{\text{model}})+\mathrm{KL}(q_{\text{out}}\|p_{\text{target}}) (40)

This matches the main text.

The KL Divergence Identity for Normalizing Flows

A key property of normalizing flows is the invariance of KL divergence under invertible transformations, specifically relating the KL divergence at the input of a layer to the KL divergence at its output. We aim to show:

KL(qin∥pmodel)=KL(qout∥ptarget)\mathrm{KL}(q_{\text{in}}\|p_{\text{model}})=\mathrm{KL}(q_{\text{out}}\|p_{\text{target}}) (41)

Recall that qin​(𝐱)q_{\text{in}}({\mathbf{x}}) is the actual density of the layer’s input and qout​(𝐲)q_{\text{out}}({\mathbf{y}}) is the actual density of the layer’s output, where 𝐲=f⁡(𝐱){\mathbf{y}}=f({\mathbf{x}}). These are related by the change of variables formula:

qin​(𝐱)=qout​(f⁡(𝐱))​|detJf​(𝐱)|q_{\text{in}}({\mathbf{x}})=q_{\text{out}}(f({\mathbf{x}}))\left|\det J_{f}({\mathbf{x}})\right| (42)

Similarly, pmodel​(𝐱|cond)p_{\text{model}}({\mathbf{x}}|\text{cond}) is the density parameterized by the layer for its input, and ptarget​(𝐲)p_{\text{target}}({\mathbf{y}}) is the fixed target density for the output. The transformation ff is constructed such that these are also related by the change of variables formula:

pmodel​(𝐱|cond)=ptarget​(f⁡(𝐱))​|detJf​(𝐱)|p_{\text{model}}({\mathbf{x}}|\text{cond})=p_{\text{target}}(f({\mathbf{x}}))\left|\det J_{f}({\mathbf{x}})\right| (43)

Now, consider the ratio qin​(𝐱)pmodel​(𝐱|cond)\frac{q_{\text{in}}({\mathbf{x}})}{p_{\text{model}}({\mathbf{x}}|\text{cond})}:

qin​(𝐱)pmodel​(𝐱|cond)=qout​(f⁡(𝐱))​|detJf​(𝐱)|ptarget​(f⁡(𝐱))​|detJf​(𝐱)|=qout​(f​(𝐱))ptarget​(f​(𝐱))\frac{q_{\text{in}}({\mathbf{x}})}{p_{\text{model}}({\mathbf{x}}|\text{cond})}=\frac{q_{\text{out}}(f({\mathbf{x}}))\left|\det J_{f}({\mathbf{x}})\right|}{p_{\text{target}}(f({\mathbf{x}}))\left|\det J_{f}({\mathbf{x}})\right|}=\frac{q_{\text{out}}(f({\mathbf{x}}))}{p_{\text{target}}(f({\mathbf{x}}))} (44)

The KL divergence KL(qin∥pmodel)\mathrm{KL}(q_{\text{in}}\|p_{\text{model}}) is defined as:

KL(qin∥pmodel)=∫qin(𝐱)logqin​(𝐱)pmodel​(𝐱|cond)d𝐱\mathrm{KL}(q_{\text{in}}\|p_{\text{model}})=\int q_{\text{in}}({\mathbf{x}})\log\frac{q_{\text{in}}({\mathbf{x}})}{p_{\text{model}}({\mathbf{x}}|\text{cond})}d{\mathbf{x}} (45)

Substitute Eq. equation 44 into the logarithm:

KL(qin∥pmodel)=∫qin(𝐱)logqout​(f​(𝐱))ptarget​(f​(𝐱))d𝐱\mathrm{KL}(q_{\text{in}}\|p_{\text{model}})=\int q_{\text{in}}({\mathbf{x}})\log\frac{q_{\text{out}}(f({\mathbf{x}}))}{p_{\text{target}}(f({\mathbf{x}}))}d{\mathbf{x}} (46)

Now, perform a change of variables in the integration from 𝐱{\mathbf{x}} to 𝐲=f⁡(𝐱){\mathbf{y}}=f({\mathbf{x}}). We have 𝐱=f−1​(𝐲){\mathbf{x}}=f^{-1}({\mathbf{y}}), and d​𝐱=|detJf−1​(𝐲)|​d​𝐲d{\mathbf{x}}=\left|\det J_{f^{-1}}({\mathbf{y}})\right|d{\mathbf{y}}. The integral becomes:

KL(qin∥pmodel)=∫qin(f−1(𝐲))logqout​(𝐲)ptarget​(𝐲)|detJf−1(𝐲)|d𝐲\mathrm{KL}(q_{\text{in}}\|p_{\text{model}})=\int q_{\text{in}}(f^{-1}({\mathbf{y}}))\log\frac{q_{\text{out}}({\mathbf{y}})}{p_{\text{target}}({\mathbf{y}})}\left|\det J_{f^{-1}}({\mathbf{y}})\right|d{\mathbf{y}} (47)

From the change of variables for qinq_{\text{in}} (Eq. equation 42, rearranged for f−1f^{-1}), we know that qin​(f−1​(𝐲))​|detJf−1​(𝐲)|=qout​(𝐲)q_{\text{in}}(f^{-1}({\mathbf{y}}))\left|\det J_{f^{-1}}({\mathbf{y}})\right|=q_{\text{out}}({\mathbf{y}}). Substituting this into the integral:

KL(qin∥pmodel)=∫qout(𝐲)logqout​(𝐲)ptarget​(𝐲)d𝐲\mathrm{KL}(q_{\text{in}}\|p_{\text{model}})=\int q_{\text{out}}({\mathbf{y}})\log\frac{q_{\text{out}}({\mathbf{y}})}{p_{\text{target}}({\mathbf{y}})}d{\mathbf{y}} (48)

The right-hand side is, by definition, KL(qout∥ptarget)\mathrm{KL}(q_{\text{out}}\|p_{\text{target}}). Thus, the identity in Eq. equation 41 is established.

Final Expression for Expected Log-Jacobian

Substituting the KL divergence identity (Eq. equation 41) into the expanded expression for 𝒥layer\mathcal{J}_{\text{layer}} (Eq. equation 40):

𝒥layer\displaystyle\mathcal{J}_{\text{layer}} =H(qout)−H(qin)−KL(qin∥pmodel)+KL(qin∥pmodel)\displaystyle=H(q_{\text{out}})-H(q_{\text{in}})-\mathrm{KL}(q_{\text{in}}\|p_{\text{model}})+\mathrm{KL}(q_{\text{in}}\|p_{\text{model}}) (49)
=H⁡(qout)−H⁡(qin)\displaystyle=H(q_{\text{out}})-H(q_{\text{in}}) (50)

This confirms the results the main text: the expected log-determinant of the Jacobian for an invertible transformation is the change in differential entropy from its input distribution to its output distribution.

Interpretation of the Learning Objective for a Single Layer

The overall ELBO maximization drives the learning of parameters 𝜽{\bm{\theta}}, which include the parameters defining pmodel​(𝐱|cond)p_{\text{model}}({\mathbf{x}}|\text{cond}) for each layer. The contribution of a single layer’s Jacobian to the ELBO is 𝒥layer=H⁡(qout)−H⁡(qin)\mathcal{J}_{\text{layer}}=H(q_{\text{out}})-H(q_{\text{in}}).

However, the parameters of the current layer ff directly influence pmodel​(𝐱|cond)p_{\text{model}}({\mathbf{x}}|\text{cond}). To maximize 𝒥layer\mathcal{J}_{\text{layer}}, consider its expression before the KL terms cancel: 𝒥layer=H(qout)−H(qin)−KL(qin∥pmodel)+KL(qout∥ptarget)\mathcal{J}_{\text{layer}}=H(q_{\text{out}})-H(q_{\text{in}})-\mathrm{KL}(q_{\text{in}}\|p_{\text{model}})+\mathrm{KL}(q_{\text{out}}\|p_{\text{target}}). Using the identity KL(qin∥pmodel)=KL(qout∥ptarget)\mathrm{KL}(q_{\text{in}}\|p_{\text{model}})=\mathrm{KL}(q_{\text{out}}\|p_{\text{target}}), this is also: 𝒥layer=𝔼qin​(𝐱)​[log⁡pmodel​(𝐱|cond)]−𝔼qout​(𝐲)​[log⁡ptarget​(𝐲)]\mathcal{J}_{\text{layer}}=\mathbb{E}_{q_{\text{in}}({\mathbf{x}})}\left[\log p_{\text{model}}({\mathbf{x}}|\text{cond})\right]-\mathbb{E}_{q_{\text{out}}({\mathbf{y}})}\left[\log p_{\text{target}}({\mathbf{y}})\right].

The optimization process adjusts the parameters of ff (which define pmodelp_{\text{model}}) to maximize this quantity. Maximizing 𝔼qin​(𝐱)​[log⁡pmodel​(𝐱|cond)]\mathbb{E}_{q_{\text{in}}({\mathbf{x}})}\left[\log p_{\text{model}}({\mathbf{x}}|\text{cond})\right] is equivalent to minimizing KL(qin∥pmodel)\mathrm{KL}(q_{\text{in}}\|p_{\text{model}}) (since −H⁡(qin)-H(q_{\text{in}}) does not depend on the parameters of the current layer ff, but rather on the data and preceding layers/encoder). When KL(qin∥pmodel)\mathrm{KL}(q_{\text{in}}\|p_{\text{model}}) is minimized, pmodel​(𝐱|cond)p_{\text{model}}({\mathbf{x}}|\text{cond}) becomes a good approximation of the actual input distribution qin​(𝐱)q_{\text{in}}({\mathbf{x}}).

Due to the identity KL(qin∥pmodel)=KL(qout∥ptarget)\mathrm{KL}(q_{\text{in}}\|p_{\text{model}})=\mathrm{KL}(q_{\text{out}}\|p_{\text{target}}), minimizing KL(qin∥pmodel)\mathrm{KL}(q_{\text{in}}\|p_{\text{model}}) simultaneously implies minimizing KL(qout∥ptarget)\mathrm{KL}(q_{\text{out}}\|p_{\text{target}}). This means that the actual output distribution qout​(𝐲)q_{\text{out}}({\mathbf{y}}) is driven to match the fixed target distribution ptarget​(𝐲)p_{\text{target}}({\mathbf{y}}).

In summary, each flow layer learns to:

  1. 1.

    Model its input distribution: The layer’s parameters (defining pmodel​(𝐱|cond)p_{\text{model}}({\mathbf{x}}|\text{cond})) are adjusted so that pmodel​(𝐱|cond)p_{\text{model}}({\mathbf{x}}|\text{cond}) accurately represents the distribution qin​(𝐱)q_{\text{in}}({\mathbf{x}}) of the data it receives. This corresponds to minimizing KL(qin∥pmodel)\mathrm{KL}(q_{\text{in}}\|p_{\text{model}}).

  2. 2.

    Transform its input to a target distribution: As a consequence of (1) and the construction of ff, the layer transforms its input 𝐱{\mathbf{x}} into an output 𝐲{\mathbf{y}} whose distribution qout​(𝐲)q_{\text{out}}({\mathbf{y}}) closely matches the predefined target distribution ptarget​(𝐲)p_{\text{target}}({\mathbf{y}}). This corresponds to minimizing KL(qout∥ptarget)\mathrm{KL}(q_{\text{out}}\|p_{\text{target}}).

This step-by-step process, repeated through the stack of flow layers, allows the overall normalizing flow to transform a complex data distribution into a simple base distribution (e.g., standard Gaussian), while enabling exact density calculation.

Appendix D 11-D Mixture-of-Gaussian and Mixture-of-Logistics Coupling

The analysis in main text show that can be AR MoG prob distribution interpreted as an implicit normalizing flow layer. This layer utilizes the cumulative distribution function (CDF) of the Gaussian mixture to map between the data space 𝐮t{\mathbf{u}}_{t} and a base space (implicitly standard normal). Similar transformations, built explicitly around mixture CDFs, are employed in various normalizing flow architectures. This section provides a detailed comparison between the transformation implicitly defined by our model and common explicit parameterizations, establishing their functional equivalence. We will consistently analyze the transformations in the **data-to-latent** direction for clarity, and then briefly discuss the inverse (latent-to-data) direction.

For conciseness within this section, we may drop the time index tt and dimension index ii from variables and parameters when the context is clear (e.g., using xx for a single data dimension, ϵ\epsilon or ww for the corresponding latent dimension, and πk,μk,σk\pi_{k},\mu_{k},\sigma_{k} for the mixture parameters predicted based on history). We maintain the standard normal PDF φ⁡(⋅)\varphi(\cdot) and CDF Φ⁡(⋅)\Phi(\cdot), and the standard logistic CDF σ⁡(r)=1/(1+e−r)\sigma(r)=1/(1+e^{-r}) and its inverse, the logit function σ−1​(p)=log⁡(p/(1−p))\sigma^{-1}(p)=\log(p/(1-p)).

The Core Component: Gaussian Mixture CDF.

Both the implicit and explicit layers rely on the same core component: the CDF of the Gaussian mixture distribution. For a single data dimension xx, the mixture CDF Fmix​(x)F_{\text{mix}}(x), conditioned on history (parameters πk,μk,σk\pi_{k},\mu_{k},\sigma_{k}), is:

Fmix​(x)=∑k=1V′πk​Φ​(x−μkσk)F_{\text{mix}}(x)=\sum_{k=1}^{V^{\prime}}\pi_{k}\Phi\left(\frac{x-\mu_{k}}{\sigma_{k}}\right) (51)

The derivative of this CDF with respect to xx is the probability density function (PDF) of the mixture:

m⁡(x)=d​Fmix​(x)d​x=∑k=1V′πk​φ​(x−μkσk)​1σkm(x)=\frac{dF_{\text{mix}}(x)}{dx}=\sum_{k=1}^{V^{\prime}}\pi_{k}\varphi\left(\frac{x-\mu_{k}}{\sigma_{k}}\right)\frac{1}{\sigma_{k}} (52)

This mixture PDF m⁡(x)m(x) plays a key role in the Jacobian determinant calculations.

Layer Definitions and Jacobians (Data-to-Latent Direction).

We now define two primary variants of the mixture CDF transformation layer, both mapping the data variable xx to a latent variable, but differing in the choice of outer non-linearity and corresponding base distribution.

MoG Variant: ProbitMixtureCDF

This layer corresponds to the transformation gt,ig_{t,i} identified in Section Sec. 3.2.2. It maps the data xx to a latent variable zz, assumed to follow a standard normal distribution 𝒩⁡(0,1)\mathcal{N}(0,1).

z=Φ−1​(Fmix​(x))z=\Phi^{-1}(F_{\text{mix}}(x)) (53)

Its Jacobian determinant, ∂z/∂x\partial z/\partial x, is calculated using the chain rule and properties of Φ−1\Phi^{-1} and FmixF_{\text{mix}} :

∂z∂x=m⁡(x)φ⁡(z)\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}=\frac{m(x)}{\varphi(z)} (54)

The log-Jacobian determinant is therefore:

log⁡|∂z∂x|=log⁡m⁡(x)−log⁡φ⁡(z)\log\left|\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right|=\log m(x)-\log\varphi(z) (55)
MoL Variant: LogitMixtureCDF

Explicit flow layers often use the logit function σ−1\sigma^{-1} as the outer non-linearity, mapping the probability Fmix​(x)F_{\text{mix}}(x) to a latent variable ww, typically assumed to follow a standard logistic distribution. We consider the core transformation without additional affine terms for now:

w=σ−1​(Fmix​(x))w=\sigma^{-1}(F_{\text{mix}}(x)) (56)

Its Jacobian determinant, ∂w/∂x\partial w/\partial x, is calculated using the chain rule. The derivative of σ−1​(p)\sigma^{-1}(p) is 1/(p⁡(1−p))1/(p(1-p)). The PDF of the standard logistic distribution is plogistic​(w)=σ′​(w)=σ⁡(w)​(1−σ⁡(w))p_{\text{logistic}}(w)=\sigma^{\prime}(w)=\sigma(w)(1-\sigma(w)). Since Fmix​(x)=σ​(w)F_{\text{mix}}(x)=\sigma(w), we have Fmix​(x)​(1−Fmix​(x))=plogistic​(w)F_{\text{mix}}(x)(1-F_{\text{mix}}(x))=p_{\text{logistic}}(w).

∂w∂x=d​σ−1​(p)d​p|p=Fmix​(x)⋅d​Fmix​(x)d​x=1Fmix​(x)​(1−Fmix​(x))⋅m⁡(x)=m⁡(x)plogistic​(w)\frac{\partial w}{\partial x}=\frac{d\sigma^{-1}(p)}{dp}\Bigg|_{p=F_{\text{mix}}(x)}\cdot\frac{dF_{\text{mix}}(x)}{dx}=\frac{1}{F_{\text{mix}}(x)(1-F_{\text{mix}}(x))}\cdot m(x)=\frac{m(x)}{p_{\text{logistic}}(w)} (57)

The log-Jacobian determinant is therefore:

log⁡|∂w∂x|=log⁡m⁡(x)−log⁡plogistic​(w)\log\left|\frac{\partial w}{\partial x}\right|=\log m(x)-\log p_{\text{logistic}}(w) (58)
Comparison in the Data-to-Latent Direction.

Table 4 summarizes the two variants when viewed in the data-to-latent direction.

Both transformations share the same initial structure involving Fmix​(x)F_{\text{mix}}(x) and yield a log-Jacobian determinant of the form log⁡m⁡(x)−log⁡pbase​(latent)\log m(x)-\log p_{\text{base}}(\text{latent}), where pbasep_{\text{base}} is the PDF of the corresponding base distribution (Gaussian or Logistic). The difference lies solely in the choice of the outer bijection (Φ−1\Phi^{-1} vs σ−1\sigma^{-1}) and the associated base distribution.

Connecting the Variants via Re-parameterization.

The Probit and Logit variants are functionally equivalent because the standard normal and standard logistic distributions can be transformed into one another via a simple, smooth, invertible function. Define the map g:ℝ→ℝg:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} that converts a standard logistic variable ww into a standard normal variable zz:

z=g⁡(w)=Φ−1​(σ⁡(w))z=g(w)=\Phi^{-1}(\sigma(w)) (59)

The inverse map g−1:ℝ→ℝg^{-1}:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} converts a standard normal variable zz into a standard logistic variable ww:

w=g−1​(z)=σ−1​(Φ⁡(z))w=g^{-1}(z)=\sigma^{-1}(\Phi(z)) (60)

These functions act as translators between the two latent spaces.

We can demonstrate the equivalence by composing one layer type with the appropriate function gg or g−1g^{-1}:

  • •

    LogitMixtureCDF followed by gg: If we take the output ww from the LogitMixtureCDF layer (Eq. equation 56) and apply gg, we get:

    g⁡(w)=g⁡(σ−1​(Fmix​(x)))=Φ−1​(σ⁡(σ−1​(Fmix​(x))))=Φ−1​(Fmix​(x))g(w)=g(\sigma^{-1}(F_{\text{mix}}(x)))=\Phi^{-1}(\sigma(\sigma^{-1}(F_{\text{mix}}(x))))=\Phi^{-1}(F_{\text{mix}}(x)) (61)

    This result is exactly the output zz of the ProbitMixtureCDF layer (Eq. equation 53).

  • •

    ProbitMixtureCDF followed by g−1g^{-1}: If we take the output zz from the ProbitMixtureCDF layer (Eq. equation 53) and apply g−1g^{-1}, we get:

    g−1​(z)=g−1​(Φ−1​(Fmix​(x)))=σ−1​(Φ⁡(Φ−1​(Fmix​(x))))=σ−1​(Fmix​(x))g^{-1}(z)=g^{-1}(\Phi^{-1}(F_{\text{mix}}(x)))=\sigma^{-1}(\Phi(\Phi^{-1}(F_{\text{mix}}(x))))=\sigma^{-1}(F_{\text{mix}}(x)) (62)

    This result is exactly the output ww of the LogitMixtureCDF layer (Eq. equation 56).

This shows that the two layer types are related by composition with the fixed, invertible function gg. In the context of normalizing flows, composing with such a function simply constitutes another valid flow layer, effectively re-parameterizing the latent space without changing the transformation’s overall expressive power on the data xx.

Likelihood Equivalence.

The equivalence is further confirmed by examining the data log-likelihood log⁡p⁡(x)\log p(x) induced by each transformation. Using the change of variables formula for the data-to-latent direction z=T−1​(x)z=T^{-1}(x): log⁡p⁡(x)=log⁡pbase​(z)+log⁡|detJT−1​(x)|\log p(x)=\log p_{\text{base}}(z)+\log|\det J_{T^{-1}}(x)|.

  • •

    ProbitMixtureCDF:

    log⁡p⁡(x)\displaystyle\log p(x) =log⁡pgaussian​(z)+log⁡|∂z∂x|\displaystyle=\log p_{\text{gaussian}}(z)+\log\left|\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right|
    =log⁡φ⁡(z)+(log⁡m⁡(x)−log⁡φ⁡(z))=log⁡m⁡(x)\displaystyle=\log\varphi(z)+(\log m(x)-\log\varphi(z))=\log m(x) (63)
  • •

    LogitMixtureCDF:

    log⁡p⁡(x)\displaystyle\log p(x) =log⁡plogistic​(w)+log⁡|∂w∂x|\displaystyle=\log p_{\text{logistic}}(w)+\log\left|\frac{\partial w}{\partial x}\right|
    =log⁡plogistic​(w)+(log⁡m⁡(x)−log⁡plogistic​(w))=log⁡m⁡(x)\displaystyle=\log p_{\text{logistic}}(w)+(\log m(x)-\log p_{\text{logistic}}(w))=\log m(x) (64)

Both formulations yield log⁡p⁡(x)=log⁡m⁡(x)\log p(x)=\log m(x), the log-PDF of the Gaussian mixture model defining the transformation. The contribution from the base density’s log-PDF always exactly cancels the second term in the layer’s log-Jacobian determinant. This confirms that both variants define the exact same probability distribution over the data xx, given the same mixture parameters (πk,μk,σk)(\pi_{k},\mu_{k},\sigma_{k}). Consequently, the gradients with respect to these parameters during training will be identical.

Handling Affine Transformations.

Explicit layers like the GaussMixCDF snippet often include an affine transformation y=ea​w+by=e^{a}w+b applied after the core logit transformation w=σ−1​(Fmix​(x))w=\sigma^{-1}(F_{\text{mix}}(x)). This affine transformation is itself an invertible flow layer with a simple constant log-Jacobian determinant:

log⁡|∂y∂w|=log⁡|ea|=a\log\left|\frac{\partial y}{\partial w}\right|=\log|e^{a}|=a (65)

This term simply adds aa to the total log-determinant of the composed flow (x→w→yx\to w\to y). Such affine transformations do not change the core functionality related to the mixture CDF and can be treated as separate layers (like Batch Normalization or ActNorm layers) or fused for implementation. Their presence or absence does not affect the fundamental equivalence discussed above.

Latent-to-Data Direction.

For completeness, we consider the inverse (generative) direction, mapping the latent variable back to the data xx.

MoG Variant: ProbitMixtureCDF Inverse This corresponds to the transformation hh:

x=h⁡(z)=Fmix−1​(Φ⁡(z))x=h(z)=F_{\text{mix}}^{-1}(\Phi(z)) (66)

The log-Jacobian is the negative of the forward log-Jacobian (Eq. equation 55):

log⁡|∂x∂z|=−(log⁡m⁡(x)−log⁡φ⁡(z))=log⁡φ⁡(z)−log⁡m⁡(x)\log\left|\frac{\partial x}{\partial z}\right|=-(\log m(x)-\log\varphi(z))=\log\varphi(z)-\log m(x) (67)

MoL Variant: LogitMixtureCDF Inverse Inverting w=σ−1​(Fmix​(x))w=\sigma^{-1}(F_{\text{mix}}(x)) gives Fmix​(x)=σ​(w)F_{\text{mix}}(x)=\sigma(w), so:

x=Fmix−1​(σ⁡(w))x=F_{\text{mix}}^{-1}(\sigma(w)) (68)

The log-Jacobian is the negative of the forward log-Jacobian (Eq. equation 58):

log⁡|∂x∂w|=−(log⁡m⁡(x)−log⁡plogistic​(w))=log⁡plogistic​(w)−log⁡m⁡(x)\log\left|\frac{\partial x}{\partial w}\right|=-(\log m(x)-\log p_{\text{logistic}}(w))=\log p_{\text{logistic}}(w)-\log m(x) (69)

Table 5 summarizes the inverse transformations.

The transformation implicitly defined by our AR-MDN base prior is functionally equivalent to explicit Gaussian Mixture CDF flow layers found in the literature. Both leverage the mixture CDF FmixF_{\text{mix}} to perform a complex, data-dependent monotonic transformation. Differences in the choice of outer bijection (probit vs. logit) and associated base distributions (Gaussian vs. logistic), as well as optional affine components, amount to implementation choices or re-parameterizations connected by the simple diffeomorphism gg. They represent the same class of transformations and induce the same probability density on the data xx for identical mixture parameters. Our VAE approach benefits from this expressive power implicitly by optimizing the mixture density p⁡(𝐮t|𝐮<t)=m⁡(𝐮t)p({\mathbf{u}}_{t}|{\mathbf{u}}_{<t})=m({\mathbf{u}}_{t}) directly, avoiding the potentially costly computation of Fmix−1F_{\text{mix}}^{-1}, Φ−1\Phi^{-1}, or σ−1\sigma^{-1} during training.

Appendix E Additional Experimental Results

This section provides supplementary experimental details and results that support the findings presented in the main body of the paper.

Fig. 8 offers a more complete view of the training and validation loss curves, expanding on the comparison shown in Fig. 3 of the main text. These curves illustrate the learning progression for different model configurations. The results underscore the benefit of incorporating mixture-based coupling layers, which exhibit improved convergence and final performance (lower negative ELBO) compared to configurations relying solely on standard affine coupling layers. This observation reinforces the point made in the main text regarding the importance of mixture couplings for effectively modeling discrete text data within our continuous latent space framework.

To further clarify the mechanics of our proposed model variants, Alg. 1 details the forward transformation process for the dd-dimensional mixture flow layer. This transformation is a core component of the ‘Mix-d‘ model configuration (discussed in Section 3.2.2), enabling the direct modeling of token-wise dependencies in a dd-dimensional latent space using a mixture of Gaussians. The algorithm outlines how an input vector 𝐳{\mathbf{z}} is mapped to an output vector 𝐮{\mathbf{u}} that follows a standard Gaussian distribution, through a sequence of conditional 1D mixture-CDF transformations.

Alg. 2 describes the channel mixing and unmixing operations. These procedures are employed in the context of block-wise multi-token generation, as discussed in the "Flexible Patch Size" paragraph of the experiments section. By permuting latent dimensions between flow layers, channel mixing facilitates information exchange across different token positions within a patch, allowing the model to capture intra-patch dependencies more effectively as data propagates through the stack of flow transformations. The ChannelUnmix procedure is the exact inverse, ensuring the overall transformation remains bijective.

Appendix F Connection to Discrete Autoregressive Language Models

A specific configuration of our continuous latent space framework reveals a direct relationship with conventional discrete autoregressive language models. This connection arises when we consider the model structure outlined in Section 3 under particular assumptions for the prior p(𝐳1:T)p({\mathbf{z}}_{1:T}) and the encoder/decoder.

Specifically, we focus on the token-wise autoregressive prior for p(𝐳1:T)p({\mathbf{z}}_{1:T}) as factorized in Section 3.2, where each conditional p⁡(𝐳t|𝐳<t)p({\mathbf{z}}_{t}|{\mathbf{z}}_{<t}) is modeled as a dd-dimensional mixture of Gaussians. We adopt the formulation from Eq. equation 7, where a shared codebook of Gaussian components is used. The key assumptions for this connection are: Tied Prior and Encoder Components: The VV Gaussian components {𝝁kprior,(σkprior)2}k=1V\{\bm{\mu}_{k}^{\text{prior}},(\sigma_{k}^{\text{prior}})^{2}\}_{k=1}^{V} used in the prior p⁡(𝐳t|𝐳<t)p({\mathbf{z}}_{t}|{\mathbf{z}}_{<t}) are identical to the VAE encoder’s Gaussian components {𝝁k,σk2}k=1V\{{\bm{\mu}}_{k},\sigma_{k}^{2}\}_{k=1}^{V} defined in Section 3.1 (Eq. equation 3.1). Thus, VV equals the vocabulary size, 𝝁kprior=𝝁k\bm{\mu}_{k}^{\text{prior}}={\bm{\mu}}_{k}, and (σkprior)2=σk2(\sigma_{k}^{\text{prior}})^{2}=\sigma_{k}^{2}. The prior conditional then becomes:

p⁡(𝐳t|𝐳<t)=∑k=1V𝝅t​(𝐳<t)​[k]​𝒩​(𝐳t,𝝁k,σk2​𝑰)=∑k=1V𝝅t​(𝐳<t)​[k]​𝒩k​(𝐳t)p({\mathbf{z}}_{t}|{\mathbf{z}}_{<t})=\sum_{k=1}^{V}\bm{\pi}_{t}({\mathbf{z}}_{<t})[k]\mathcal{N}({\mathbf{z}}_{t};{\bm{\mu}}_{k},\sigma_{k}^{2}{\bm{I}})=\sum_{k=1}^{V}\bm{\pi}_{t}({\mathbf{z}}_{<t})[k]\mathcal{N}_{k}({\mathbf{z}}_{t}) (70)

where 𝝅t​(𝐳<t)\bm{\pi}_{t}({\mathbf{z}}_{<t}) are the mixture weights predicted by a Transformer based on the history 𝐳<t{\mathbf{z}}_{<t}. Tied Encoder-Decoder: The decoder p⁡(xt|𝐳t)p(x_{t}|{\mathbf{z}}_{t}) uses the tied Bayesian formulation from Eq. equation 3.1:

p⁡(xt=k|𝐳t)=𝒩k​(𝐳t)∑j=1V𝒩j​(𝐳t)p(x_{t}=k|{\mathbf{z}}_{t})=\frac{\mathcal{N}_{k}({\mathbf{z}}_{t})}{\sum_{j=1}^{V}\mathcal{N}_{j}({\mathbf{z}}_{t})} (71)

No Additional Flow Transformations for Prior: We consider the case where the prior p(𝐳1:T)=∏tp(𝐳t|𝐳<t)p({\mathbf{z}}_{1:T})=\prod_{t}p({\mathbf{z}}_{t}|{\mathbf{z}}_{<t}) with p⁡(𝐳t|𝐳<t)p({\mathbf{z}}_{t}|{\mathbf{z}}_{<t}) defined by Eq. equation 70 is used directly in the ELBO (Eq. equation 3). This corresponds to setting L=0L=0 in the context of stacked flow layers (Section 3.3), meaning 𝐳1:T{\mathbf{z}}_{1:T} is not further transformed into 𝐮1:T{\mathbf{u}}_{1:T} via additional flow layers for this analysis.

Under these conditions, the ELBO (Eq. equation 3) is maximized. Let’s analyze the terms in the ELBO related to a single token xtx_{t}, given its history 𝐱<t{\mathbf{x}}_{<t}. The relevant part of the ELBO expectation, for a sample 𝐳1:T∼q(⋅|𝐱1:T){\mathbf{z}}_{1:T}\sim q(\cdot|{\mathbf{x}}_{1:T}), can be written per token tt as:

ℒteff=log⁡p⁡(xt|𝐳t)+log⁡p⁡(𝐳t|𝐳<t)−log⁡q⁡(𝐳t|xt)\mathcal{L}_{t}^{\text{eff}}=\log p(x_{t}|{\mathbf{z}}_{t})+\log p({\mathbf{z}}_{t}|{\mathbf{z}}_{<t})-\log q({\mathbf{z}}_{t}|x_{t}) (72)

Substituting the definitions:

ℒteff\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{t}^{\text{eff}} =log⁡(𝒩xt​(𝐳t)∑j=1V𝒩j​(𝐳t))+log⁡(∑k=1V𝝅t​(𝐳<t)​[k]​𝒩k​(𝐳t))−log⁡𝒩xt​(𝐳t)\displaystyle=\log\left(\frac{\mathcal{N}_{x_{t}}({\mathbf{z}}_{t})}{\sum_{j=1}^{V}\mathcal{N}_{j}({\mathbf{z}}_{t})}\right)+\log\left(\sum_{k=1}^{V}\bm{\pi}_{t}({\mathbf{z}}_{<t})[k]\mathcal{N}_{k}({\mathbf{z}}_{t})\right)-\log\mathcal{N}_{x_{t}}({\mathbf{z}}_{t}) (73)
=log⁡𝒩xt​(𝐳t)−log⁡(∑j=1V𝒩j​(𝐳t))+log⁡(∑k=1V𝝅t​(𝐳<t)​[k]​𝒩k​(𝐳t))−log⁡𝒩xt​(𝐳t)\displaystyle=\log\mathcal{N}_{x_{t}}({\mathbf{z}}_{t})-\log\left(\sum_{j=1}^{V}\mathcal{N}_{j}({\mathbf{z}}_{t})\right)+\log\left(\sum_{k=1}^{V}\bm{\pi}_{t}({\mathbf{z}}_{<t})[k]\mathcal{N}_{k}({\mathbf{z}}_{t})\right)-\log\mathcal{N}_{x_{t}}({\mathbf{z}}_{t}) (74)
=log⁡(∑k=1V𝝅t​(𝐳<t)​[k]​𝒩k​(𝐳t))−log⁡(∑j=1V𝒩j​(𝐳t))\displaystyle=\log\left(\sum_{k=1}^{V}\bm{\pi}_{t}({\mathbf{z}}_{<t})[k]\mathcal{N}_{k}({\mathbf{z}}_{t})\right)-\log\left(\sum_{j=1}^{V}\mathcal{N}_{j}({\mathbf{z}}_{t})\right)
=log⁡(∑k=1V𝝅t​(𝐳<t)​[k]​𝒩k​(𝐳t)∑j=1V𝒩j​(𝐳t))\displaystyle=\log\left(\sum_{k=1}^{V}\bm{\pi}_{t}({\mathbf{z}}_{<t})[k]\frac{\mathcal{N}_{k}({\mathbf{z}}_{t})}{\sum_{j=1}^{V}\mathcal{N}_{j}({\mathbf{z}}_{t})}\right)
=log⁡(∑k=1V𝝅t​(𝐳<t)​[k]​p​(xt=k|𝐳t))\displaystyle=\log\left(\sum_{k=1}^{V}\bm{\pi}_{t}({\mathbf{z}}_{<t})[k]p(x_{t}=k|{\mathbf{z}}_{t})\right) (75)

The full ELBO involves an expectation 𝔼𝐳1:T∼q(⋅|𝐱1:T)[∑tℒteff]\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{z}}_{1:T}\sim q(\cdot|{\mathbf{x}}_{1:T})}[\sum_{t}\mathcal{L}_{t}^{\text{eff}}].

Proposition 4.

(Connection to Cross-Entropy Discrete AR LM). Under the tying conditions specified above (tied prior/encoder components, tied decoder, and L=0L=0 for additional flows), in the limit where the encoder/prior Gaussian components become infinitely narrow (i.e., σk2→0\sigma_{k}^{2}\to 0 for all k=1,…,Vk=1,\ldots,V), minimizing the negative of the ELBO terms related to prior prediction and reconstruction for token xtx_{t} approaches minimizing −log⁡𝛑t​(𝛍x1,…,𝛍xt−1)​[xt]-\log\bm{\pi}_{t}({\bm{\mu}}_{x_{1}},\dots,{\bm{\mu}}_{x_{t-1}})[x_{t}]. This is equivalent to the negative log-likelihood (cross-entropy) objective for a discrete autoregressive model predicting token xtx_{t} given the (deterministic embedding of) previous tokens.

Proof.

Consider the term ℒteff\mathcal{L}_{t}^{\text{eff}} from Eq. equation 75. The latent variables 𝐳t{\mathbf{z}}_{t} are sampled from q⁡(𝐳t|xt)=𝒩xt​(𝐳t)=𝒩⁡(𝐳t,𝝁xt,σxt2​𝑰)q({\mathbf{z}}_{t}|x_{t})=\mathcal{N}_{x_{t}}({\mathbf{z}}_{t})=\mathcal{N}({\mathbf{z}}_{t};{\bm{\mu}}_{x_{t}},\sigma_{x_{t}}^{2}{\bm{I}}). As σk2→0\sigma_{k}^{2}\to 0 for all kk:

  1. 1.

    For a given true token xtx_{t}, the sample 𝐳t∼𝒩xt​(𝐳t){\mathbf{z}}_{t}\sim\mathcal{N}_{x_{t}}({\mathbf{z}}_{t}) will converge in probability to its mean: 𝐳t→𝝁xt{\mathbf{z}}_{t}\to{\bm{\mu}}_{x_{t}}.

  2. 2.

    Consequently, the history 𝐳<t=(𝐳1,…,𝐳t−1){\mathbf{z}}_{<t}=({\mathbf{z}}_{1},\ldots,{\mathbf{z}}_{t-1}) will converge to (𝝁x1,…,𝝁xt−1)({\bm{\mu}}_{x_{1}},\ldots,{\bm{\mu}}_{x_{t-1}}).

  3. 3.

    The decoder probability p⁡(xt=k|𝐳t)p(x_{t}=k|{\mathbf{z}}_{t}) (Eq. equation 71) evaluated at 𝐳t≈𝝁xt{\mathbf{z}}_{t}\approx{\bm{\mu}}_{x_{t}} will behave as follows: If 𝝁k{\bm{\mu}}_{k} are distinct, then for 𝐳t≈𝝁xt{\mathbf{z}}_{t}\approx{\bm{\mu}}_{x_{t}}, 𝒩xt​(𝐳t)\mathcal{N}_{x_{t}}({\mathbf{z}}_{t}) will be large, while 𝒩j​(𝐳t)\mathcal{N}_{j}({\mathbf{z}}_{t}) for j≠xtj\neq x_{t} will be very small. Thus, p⁡(xt=k|𝐳t≈𝝁xt)→{1if ​k=xt0if ​k≠xtp(x_{t}=k|{\mathbf{z}}_{t}\approx{\bm{\mu}}_{x_{t}})\to\begin{cases}1&\text{if }k=x_{t}\\ 0&\text{if }k\neq x_{t}\end{cases}.

Substituting these limits into Eq. equation 75, the sum ∑k=1V𝝅t​(𝐳<t)​[k]​p​(xt=k|𝐳t)\sum_{k=1}^{V}\bm{\pi}_{t}({\mathbf{z}}_{<t})[k]p(x_{t}=k|{\mathbf{z}}_{t}) becomes:

𝝅t​(𝝁x1,…,𝝁xt−1)​[xt]⋅1+∑k≠xt𝝅t​(𝝁x1,…,𝝁xt−1)​[k]⋅0=𝝅t​(𝝁x1,…,𝝁xt−1)​[xt]\bm{\pi}_{t}({\bm{\mu}}_{x_{1}},\dots,{\bm{\mu}}_{x_{t-1}})[x_{t}]\cdot 1+\sum_{k\neq x_{t}}\bm{\pi}_{t}({\bm{\mu}}_{x_{1}},\dots,{\bm{\mu}}_{x_{t-1}})[k]\cdot 0=\bm{\pi}_{t}({\bm{\mu}}_{x_{1}},\dots,{\bm{\mu}}_{x_{t-1}})[x_{t}] (76)

Therefore, in this limit, the ELBO contribution ℒteff\mathcal{L}_{t}^{\text{eff}} approaches log⁡𝝅t​(𝝁x1,…,𝝁xt−1)​[xt]\log\bm{\pi}_{t}({\bm{\mu}}_{x_{1}},\dots,{\bm{\mu}}_{x_{t-1}})[x_{t}]. Maximizing the ELBO thus involves maximizing this term, which is equivalent to minimizing its negative: −log⁡𝝅t​(𝝁x1,…,𝝁xt−1)​[xt]-\log\bm{\pi}_{t}({\bm{\mu}}_{x_{1}},\dots,{\bm{\mu}}_{x_{t-1}})[x_{t}]. This is precisely the cross-entropy loss for predicting the true token xtx_{t} given the sequence of means of the previous true tokens as context. ∎

This connection illustrates that our continuous latent variable framework, under specific simplifying assumptions (most importantly, very low-variance, well-separated encoder components and direct use of the tied mixture prior), can recover the objective of standard discrete autoregressive models. It offers a perspective on how continuous space modeling can generalize or relate to established discrete paradigms. When σk2>0\sigma_{k}^{2}>0, the objective involves a "soft" version of this cross-entropy, where the target p⁡(xt=k|𝐳t)p(x_{t}=k|{\mathbf{z}}_{t}) is not one-hot.

Appendix G Latent Space Evolution Metrics

Our framework’s formulation of language modeling within a continuous latent space, processed by stacked autoregressive normalizing flows, allows for a step-by-step observation of text formation. At any intermediate stage ℓ\ell of the LL flow transformations, the continuous latent sequence 𝐡1:T(ℓ){\mathbf{h}}_{1:T}^{(\ell)} can be decoded using the decoder to yield a corresponding textual output. This ability to materialize text from intermediate representations offers a view into how the model refines an initial latent state towards a final coherent sequence. The continuous nature of the latent variables naturally enables this step-wise refinement process. Each flow layer performs a smooth, differentiable transformation across the entire sequence representation, effectively functioning as a sophisticated editing operation. This type of fine-grained, fully learnable editing process is challenging to implement in discrete token spaces, where making intermediate adjustments typically involves solving complex discrete optimization problems.

To further characterize quantitatively the transformations, we analyze statistics of the latent codes 𝐡1:T(ℓ){\mathbf{h}}_{1:T}^{(\ell)} after each flow layer. These include: (1) the mean L2 norm of token embeddings 𝐡t(ℓ){\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}; (2) the mean pairwise cosine similarity among these embeddings within a sequence; (3) the mean Participation Ratio (PR) of the set of token embeddings {𝐡t(ℓ)}t=1T\{{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}\}_{t=1}^{T}; and (4) the mean centroid movement, measuring the Euclidean distance between the average sequence representation mean(𝐡1:T(ℓ))\text{mean}({\mathbf{h}}_{1:T}^{(\ell)}) and that of the preceding layer, mean(𝐡1:T(ℓ−1))\text{mean}({\mathbf{h}}_{1:T}^{(\ell-1)}).

Observations of these metrics reveal a structured evolution. A consistent decrease in the mean L2 norm across flow layers suggests that the transformations guide the latent representations towards a more defined and compact manifold. Simultaneously, an increasing mean pairwise cosine similarity indicates that token embeddings within a sequence become more semantically clustered, enhancing internal coherence. The utilization of embedding dimensions, can be particularly revealing when considering alternating flow directions. For example, an initial Left-to-Right (L2R) flow might establish a foundational representation with a certain value (e.g., 7). A subsequent Right-to-Left (R2L) flow could then see a drop. This reduction might occur as the R2L pass focuses on integrating suffix-based or future context, temporarily constraining the representations to a lower-dimensional manifold that captures these specific right-side dependencies. The final L2R flow, benefiting from the synthesis of both left-anchored and right-anchored information, might then exhibit a significant increase, indicating that it expands the representational capacity to integrate these now bi-directionally informed features into a richer, more expressive state. A diminishing mean centroid movement with each subsequent layer further points to a coarse-to-fine adjustment, naturally enabled by the stacked continuous transformations: initial flow layers induce larger global changes, while later layers perform more subtle, fine-tuning modifications. This hierarchical refinement is a direct benefit of operating in a continuous space where gradual adjustments are possible, unlike the often all-or-nothing choices in discrete generation.

This section provides detailed definitions and computation methods for the metrics employed to analyze the evolution of continuous latent representations 𝐡1:T(ℓ){\mathbf{h}}_{1:T}^{(\ell)} across LL stacked autoregressive flow layers. We consider a batch of BB sequences, where each sequence consists of TT tokens. The dd-dimensional latent embedding of the tt-th token in the bb-th sequence, after processing by the ℓ\ell-th flow transformation, is denoted 𝐡b,t(ℓ)∈ℝd{\mathbf{h}}_{b,t}^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. The initial state of these embeddings, prior to any flow transformations (e.g., sampled noise or an encoder’s output), is designated 𝐡b,t(0){\mathbf{h}}_{b,t}^{(0)}. The subsequent states, corresponding to the outputs of the LL flow layers, are 𝐡b,t(1),…,𝐡b,t(L){\mathbf{h}}_{b,t}^{(1)},\ldots,{\mathbf{h}}_{b,t}^{(L)}. Our statistical analysis primarily focuses on characterizing these LL flow layer outputs.

Mean L2 Norm

The L2 norm (Euclidean norm) of a token embedding 𝐡b,t(ℓ){\mathbf{h}}_{b,t}^{(\ell)} measures its magnitude in the dd-dimensional space:

‖𝐡b,t(ℓ)‖2=∑j=1d(hb,t,j(ℓ))2\|{\mathbf{h}}_{b,t}^{(\ell)}\|_{2}=\sqrt{\sum_{j=1}^{d}(h_{b,t,j}^{(\ell)})^{2}} (77)

For each sequence bb at flow layer ℓ\ell, the average L2 norm of its token embeddings is calculated as:

N¯b(ℓ)=1T​∑t=1T‖𝐡b,t(ℓ)‖2\bar{N}_{b}^{(\ell)}=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\|{\mathbf{h}}_{b,t}^{(\ell)}\|_{2} (78)

The Mean L2 Norm reported for flow layer ℓ\ell is the average of these per-sequence values over all BB sequences in the batch:

Mean L2 Norm(ℓ)=1B​∑b=1BN¯b(ℓ)\text{Mean L2 Norm}^{(\ell)}=\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\bar{N}_{b}^{(\ell)} (79)

The standard deviation of the set {N¯b(ℓ)}b=1B\{\bar{N}_{b}^{(\ell)}\}_{b=1}^{B} across the batch is also computed. This metric indicates whether the flow transformations tend to expand, contract, or preserve the overall scale of the token embeddings.

Mean Pairwise Cosine Similarity (Intra-Sequence)

Cosine similarity quantifies the angular relationship between two embedding vectors. For any two token embeddings 𝐡b,t1(ℓ){\mathbf{h}}_{b,t_{1}}^{(\ell)} and 𝐡b,t2(ℓ){\mathbf{h}}_{b,t_{2}}^{(\ell)} within the same sequence bb at flow layer ℓ\ell, their cosine similarity is:

cos_sim​(𝐡b,t1(ℓ),𝐡b,t2(ℓ))=𝐡b,t1(ℓ)⋅𝐡b,t2(ℓ)‖𝐡b,t1(ℓ)‖2​‖𝐡b,t2(ℓ)‖2+ϵcos\text{cos\_sim}({\mathbf{h}}_{b,t_{1}}^{(\ell)},{\mathbf{h}}_{b,t_{2}}^{(\ell)})=\frac{{\mathbf{h}}_{b,t_{1}}^{(\ell)}\cdot{\mathbf{h}}_{b,t_{2}}^{(\ell)}}{\|{\mathbf{h}}_{b,t_{1}}^{(\ell)}\|_{2}\|{\mathbf{h}}_{b,t_{2}}^{(\ell)}\|_{2}+\epsilon_{\text{cos}}} (80)

where ϵcos\epsilon_{\text{cos}} is a small constant (e.g., 10−910^{-9}) added to the denominator for numerical stability. For each sequence bb at flow layer ℓ\ell (assuming T>1T>1), the average cosine similarity is computed over all unique pairs of distinct tokens (t1,t2)(t_{1},t_{2}) where t1<t2t_{1}<t_{2}:

C¯b(ℓ)=2T⁡(T−1)​∑t1=1T−1∑t2=t1+1Tcos_sim​(𝐡b,t1(ℓ),𝐡b,t2(ℓ))\bar{C}_{b}^{(\ell)}=\frac{2}{T(T-1)}\sum_{t_{1}=1}^{T-1}\sum_{t_{2}=t_{1}+1}^{T}\text{cos\_sim}({\mathbf{h}}_{b,t_{1}}^{(\ell)},{\mathbf{h}}_{b,t_{2}}^{(\ell)}) (81)

If T≤1T\leq 1, this average is typically considered undefined or assigned a default value (e.g., 1.0 if T=1T=1, as there are no distinct pairs). The Mean Pairwise Cosine Similarity for flow layer ℓ\ell is the average of these per-sequence values over the batch:

Mean Pairwise Cosine Sim.(ℓ)=1B​∑b=1BC¯b(ℓ)\text{Mean Pairwise Cosine Sim.}^{(\ell)}=\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\bar{C}_{b}^{(\ell)} (82)

The standard deviation of {C¯b(ℓ)}b=1B\{\bar{C}_{b}^{(\ell)}\}_{b=1}^{B} is also reported. This metric provides insight into the internal coherence or degree of representational similarity among tokens within a sequence.

Mean Participation Ratio (PR) (Intra-Sequence)

The Participation Ratio (PR) estimates the effective number of dimensions utilized by a collection of embeddings. For a given sequence bb at flow layer ℓ\ell, let 𝐇b(ℓ)∈ℝT×d\mathbf{H}_{b}^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times d} be the matrix where each row is a token embedding 𝐡b,t(ℓ){\mathbf{h}}_{b,t}^{(\ell)}. This analysis requires T>1T>1 and d>0d>0. First, the embeddings are centered by subtracting their mean 𝐡¯b(ℓ)=1T​∑t=1T𝐡b,t(ℓ)\bar{{\mathbf{h}}}_{b}^{(\ell)}=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}{\mathbf{h}}_{b,t}^{(\ell)} from each 𝐡b,t(ℓ){\mathbf{h}}_{b,t}^{(\ell)} to obtain the centered matrix 𝐇b,centered(ℓ)\mathbf{H}_{b,\text{centered}}^{(\ell)}. The d×dd\times d sample covariance matrix of these TT centered dd-dimensional embeddings is:

Σb(ℓ)=1T−1​(𝐇b,centered(ℓ))⊤​𝐇b,centered(ℓ)\Sigma_{b}^{(\ell)}=\frac{1}{T-1}(\mathbf{H}_{b,\text{centered}}^{(\ell)})^{\top}\mathbf{H}_{b,\text{centered}}^{(\ell)} (83)

Let {λ1,…,λd}\{\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{d}\} be the non-negative eigenvalues of Σb(ℓ)\Sigma_{b}^{(\ell)}. The PR for sequence bb at layer ℓ\ell is defined as:

PRb(ℓ)=(∑j=1dλj)2∑j=1dλj2+ϵPR\text{PR}_{b}^{(\ell)}=\frac{(\sum_{j=1}^{d}\lambda_{j})^{2}}{\sum_{j=1}^{d}\lambda_{j}^{2}+\epsilon_{\text{PR}}} (84)

where ϵPR\epsilon_{\text{PR}} is a small constant to prevent division by zero if all eigenvalues are zero. The PR ranges from 1 (if all centered embeddings are collinear, indicating usage of one effective dimension) to dd (if the variance is distributed isotropically across all dd dimensions). The Mean Participation Ratio for flow layer ℓ\ell is the average over the batch:

Mean PR(ℓ)=1B​∑b=1BPRb(ℓ)\text{Mean PR}^{(\ell)}=\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\text{PR}_{b}^{(\ell)} (85)

The standard deviation of {PRb(ℓ)}b=1B\{\text{PR}_{b}^{(\ell)}\}_{b=1}^{B} is also reported. This metric indicates the breadth of the dimensional subspace actively occupied by the token representations within a sequence.

Mean Centroid Movement (Inter-Step)

The centroid of a sequence bb at a specific original step s∈{0,…,L}s\in\{0,\ldots,L\} (where s=0s=0 denotes the initial state, and s=1,…,Ls=1,\ldots,L denote the outputs of the successive flow layers) is the mean of its token embeddings at that step:

𝝁b(s)=1T​∑t=1T𝐡b,t(s){\bm{\mu}}_{b}^{(s)}=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}{\mathbf{h}}_{b,t}^{(s)} (86)

The centroid movement for sequence bb induced by the ℓ\ell-th flow layer (which transforms the representation from original step ℓ−1\ell-1 to original step ℓ\ell) is the Euclidean distance between the centroids of these two consecutive states:

Mb(ℓ)=∥𝝁b(ℓ)−𝝁b(ℓ−1)∥2,for ℓ=1,…,LM_{b}^{(\ell)}=\|{\bm{\mu}}_{b}^{(\ell)}-{\bm{\mu}}_{b}^{(\ell-1)}\|_{2},\quad\text{for }\ell=1,\ldots,L (87)

The Mean Centroid Movement for flow layer ℓ\ell is the average of these per-sequence movement magnitudes over the batch:

Mean Centroid Movement(ℓ)=1B​∑b=1BMb(ℓ)\text{Mean Centroid Movement}^{(\ell)}=\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B}M_{b}^{(\ell)} (88)

The standard deviation of {Mb(ℓ)}b=1B\{M_{b}^{(\ell)}\}_{b=1}^{B} is also reported. This metric measures the magnitude of change that each flow layer imparts on the average representation of a sequence.

Appendix H FLOPs Calculation Details

This appendix provides a detailed breakdown of how the Floating Point Operations (FLOPs) for the forward pass of an entire sequence are calculated for both the regular Transformer model and the Flow Transformer model featuring the MAF-MLP head, as presented in Figure 7. We assume a multiply-accumulate operation constitutes 2 FLOPs. FLOPs from bias terms, normalization layers, and activation functions (like GELU or ELU in the main Transformer body or within the MAF-MLP module) are generally not counted, as their contribution is typically much smaller than that of matrix multiplications.

Regular Transformer Model

The calculation for a standard autoregressive Transformer model is as follows. Let LL be the number of Transformer layers, dd be the model dimension (embedding dimension, d_model), SS be the input sequence length, and VV be the vocabulary size. We assume an MLP (Feed-Forward Network) ratio of 4, meaning the inner dimension of the FFN is 4​d4d. We also assume that the sum of attention head dimensions dattnd_{\rm attn} equals dd.

The FLOPs for each component for processing an entire sequence of length SS are:

First, for Input Embeddings (Token + Positional), each token’s embedding lookup and addition of positional encoding is approximated. For SS tokens, this is Cembed=4​d​SC_{\rm embed}=4\,d\,S.

Second, for Attention QKV Projections, for each of LL layers, input of shape (S,d)(S,d) is projected to queries, keys, and values. This can be viewed as a multiplication by a weight matrix of effective shape (d,3​d)(d,3d). FLOPs per layer: 2×S×d×3​d=6​S​d22\times S\times d\times 3d=6\,S\,d^{2}. Total for LL layers: CQKV=6​L​d2​SC_{\rm QKV}=6\,L\,d^{2}\,S.

Third, for Attention Logits (Query-Key Dot Products), in each of LL layers, each of SS query vectors (dimension dd) computes dot products with SS key vectors (dimension dd). FLOPs for one query vector to attend to all SS key vectors: S×(2​d)=2​d​SS\times(2d)=2\,d\,S. For all SS query vectors in a layer: S×(2​d​S)=2​d​S2S\times(2\,d\,S)=2\,d\,S^{2}. Total for LL layers: CQK=2​L​d​S2C_{\rm QK}=2\,L\,d\,S^{2}.

Fourth, for Attention Output Projection, for each of LL layers, the attention output (shape (S,d)(S,d)) is projected by a weight matrix of shape (d,d)(d,d). FLOPs per layer: 2×S×d×d=2​S​d22\times S\times d\times d=2\,S\,d^{2}. Total for LL layers: Cproj=2​L​d2​SC_{\rm proj}=2\,L\,d^{2}\,S.

Fifth, for Feed-Forward Network (FFN/MLP), each FFN block has two linear layers. The first linear layer (d→4​dd\to 4d): 2×S×d×4​d=8​S​d22\times S\times d\times 4d=8\,S\,d^{2}. The second linear layer (4​d→d4d\to d): 2×S×4​d×d=8​S​d22\times S\times 4d\times d=8\,S\,d^{2}. Total FFN FLOPs per layer: 16​S​d216\,S\,d^{2}. Total for LL layers: CFF=16​L​d2​SC_{\rm FF}=16\,L\,d^{2}\,S.

Finally, for Output Linear Head (De-embedding), it maps final hidden states (shape (S,d)(S,d)) to vocabulary logits (shape (S,V)(S,V)) using a weight matrix of shape (d,V)(d,V). FLOPs: Chead=2×S×d×V=2​d​V​SC_{\rm head}=2\times S\times d\times V=2\,d\,V\,S.

Summing these components, the total forward FLOPs for the entire sequence are:

Cfwd/sequenceregular\displaystyle C_{\rm fwd/sequence}^{\rm regular} =Cembed+CQKV+CQK+Cproj+CFF+Chead\displaystyle=C_{\rm embed}+C_{\rm QKV}+C_{\rm QK}+C_{\rm proj}+C_{\rm FF}+C_{\rm head}
=4​d​S+6​L​d2​S+2​L​d​S2+2​L​d2​S+16​L​d2​S+2​d​V​S\displaystyle=4\,d\,S+6\,L\,d^{2}\,S+2\,L\,d\,S^{2}+2\,L\,d^{2}\,S+16\,L\,d^{2}\,S+2\,d\,V\,S
=(6+2+16)​L​d2​S+2​L​d​S2+4​d​S+2​d​V​S\displaystyle=(6+2+16)\,L\,d^{2}\,S+2\,L\,d\,S^{2}+4\,d\,S+2\,d\,V\,S
=24​L​d2​S+2​L​d​S2+4​d​S+2​d​V​S\displaystyle=24\,L\,d^{2}\,S+2\,L\,d\,S^{2}+4\,d\,S+2\,d\,V\,S

This can be factored by SS:

Cfwd/sequenceregular=S⁡[ 24​L​d2+2​L​d​S+4​d+2​d​V]C_{\rm fwd/sequence}^{\rm regular}=S\,\Bigl[\;24\,L\,d^{2}+2\,L\,d\,S+4\,d+2\,d\,V\;\Bigr]

For the calculations related to Figure 7, the parameters LL (number of layers) and dd (model dimension) correspond to the GPT-2 configurations specified in the main text. The sequence length SS is set to 10241024, and the vocabulary size VV is 5025750257.

Flow Transformer Model (with MAF-MLP Head)

This model uses the same Transformer body as the regular model but replaces the standard linear output head with the custom MAF-MLP module. The input sequence structure is also modified based on a patch size PP.

Let LL be the number of Transformer layers in the main body, dtfd_{\rm tf} be the model dimension of the main Transformer body (i.e., n_embd from GPT-2 configs), SbaseS_{\rm base} be the original sequence length (e.g., 1024), PP be the patch size, and Sspecial=⌊Sbase/P⌋S_{\rm special}=\lfloor S_{\rm base}/P\rfloor be the effective sequence length for the Transformer body, calculated using integer division. If this value becomes 0 (e.g., if P>SbaseP>S_{\rm base}), it is clamped to 1 for calculation purposes.

The FLOPs for the Transformer body (excluding any output head) are:

Cbody/no−head=24​L​dtf2​Sspecial+2​L​dtf​Sspecial2+4​dtf​SspecialC_{\rm body/no-head}=24\,L\,d_{\rm tf}^{2}\,S_{\rm special}+2\,L\,d_{\rm tf}\,S_{\rm special}^{2}+4\,d_{\rm tf}\,S_{\rm special}

To this, we add the FLOPs from the MAF-MLP module, calculated per token and then multiplied by SspecialS_{\rm special}.

For the MAF-MLP module, let cinc_{\rm in} be the module’s input channels, determined by 16​P16P, num_mixtures=64\text{num\_mixtures}=64, cout​_​per​_​inc_{\rm out\_per\_in} be the module’s output channels per input channel, defined as 3×num_mixtures=3×64=1923\times\text{num\_mixtures}=3\times 64=192, DmoduleD_{\rm module} (the module’s hidden_size parameter, fixed at 128 for the plot) be the module’s internal hidden dimension, and EE be the module’s computed embed_size, calculated as E=min⁡(max⁡(1,int​(Dmodule×9.0/16.0/(cin−1))),96)E=\min(\max(1,\text{int}(D_{\rm module}\times 9.0/16.0/(c_{\rm in}-1))),96), where int​(⋅)\text{int}(\cdot) denotes integer casting. (We ensure cin−1>0c_{\rm in}-1>0 as P≥1⟹cin≥16P\geq 1\implies c_{\rm in}\geq 16).

The FLOPs for the MAF-MLP module (CmoduleC_{\rm module}) per token, considering only its linear layers, are:

First, the in_to_features layer projects an input of effective dimension 3​(cin−1)3(c_{\rm in}-1) to E⁡(cin−1)E(c_{\rm in}-1). FLOPs: C1=2×3​(cin−1)×E⁡(cin−1)=6​E​(cin−1)2C_{1}=2\times 3(c_{\rm in}-1)\times E(c_{\rm in}-1)=6\,E\,(c_{\rm in}-1)^{2}.

Second, the features_to_hidden layer projects an input of dimension dtf+E⁡(cin−1)d_{\rm tf}+E(c_{\rm in}-1) (concatenation of transformer output features of dimension dtfd_{\rm tf} and module’s internal in_features) to an output dimension of (Dmodule/2)​cin(D_{\rm module}/2)c_{\rm in}. FLOPs: C2=2×[dtf+E⁡(cin−1)]×(Dmodule/2×cin)=Dmodule​cin​[dtf+E⁡(cin−1)]C_{2}=2\times[d_{\rm tf}+E(c_{\rm in}-1)]\times(D_{\rm module}/2\times c_{\rm in})=D_{\rm module}\,c_{\rm in}\,[d_{\rm tf}+E(c_{\rm in}-1)].

Third, the hidden_to_out layer projects an input of dimension (Dmodule/2)​cin(D_{\rm module}/2)c_{\rm in} to cout​_​per​_​in​cinc_{\rm out\_per\_in}c_{\rm in}. FLOPs: C3=2×(Dmodule/2×cin)×(cout​_​per​_​in​cin)=Dmodule​cin2​cout​_​per​_​inC_{3}=2\times(D_{\rm module}/2\times c_{\rm in})\times(c_{\rm out\_per\_in}c_{\rm in})=D_{\rm module}\,c_{\rm in}^{2}\,c_{\rm out\_per\_in}.

The total FLOPs per token for the module is Cmodule=C1+C2+C3C_{\rm module}=C_{1}+C_{2}+C_{3}:

Cmodule=6​E​(cin−1)2+Dmodule​cin​[dtf+E⁡(cin−1)]+Dmodule​cin2​cout​_​per​_​inC_{\rm module}=6\,E\,(c_{\rm in}-1)^{2}+D_{\rm module}\,c_{\rm in}\,[d_{\rm tf}+E(c_{\rm in}-1)]+D_{\rm module}\,c_{\rm in}^{2}\,c_{\rm out\_per\_in}

The total forward FLOPs for the entire sequence in the Flow Transformer model are:

Cfwd/seqspecial\displaystyle C_{\rm fwd/seq}^{\rm special} =Cbody/no−head+Sspecial×Cmodule\displaystyle=C_{\rm body/no-head}+S_{\rm special}\times C_{\rm module}
=Sspecial​[(24​L​dtf2+2​L​dtf​Sspecial+4​dtf)+Cmodule]\displaystyle=S_{\rm special}\,\Bigl[\;(24\,L\,d_{\rm tf}^{2}+2\,L\,d_{\rm tf}\,S_{\rm special}+4\,d_{\rm tf})+C_{\rm module}\;\Bigr]

The specific parameter values used to generate the data for Figure 7 are summarized below. For the regular Transformer, the base model parameters (LL, dd, S=1024S=1024, V=50257V=50257) are taken from standard GPT-2 configurations (e.g., gpt2, gpt2-medium, gpt2-large, gpt2-xl). For the Flow Transformer (Special Transformer), the main body parameters LL and dtfd_{\rm tf} also correspond to these GPT-2 configurations. The parameters specific to its MAF-MLP head and sequence processing depend on the patch size P∈{1,2,4}P\in\{1,2,4\} as follows: Sspecial=⌊1024/P⌋S_{\rm special}=\lfloor 1024/P\rfloor (clamped to 1 if 0); cin=16​Pc_{\rm in}=16P; DmoduleD_{\rm module} (the module’s hidden_size) is 128128; num_mixtures=64\text{num\_mixtures}=64 resulting in cout​_​per​_​in=192c_{\rm out\_per\_in}=192; and E=min⁡(max⁡(1,int​(⌊Dmodule×9/(16​(cin−1))⌋)),96)E=\min(\max(1,\text{int}(\lfloor D_{\rm module}\times 9/(16\,(c_{\rm in}-1))\rfloor)),96), where int​(⋅)\text{int}(\cdot) denotes integer casting. Appendix I Related Works

Coupling-based Normalizing Flows

A substantial body of work has focused on designing expressive invertible transformations with tractable Jacobian determinants for normalizing flows. NICE [16] pioneered the use of additive coupling layers, which made the Jacobian determinant computation straightforward. RealNVP [17] built upon this by introducing scaling and shifting operations, thereby increasing model flexibility. Glow [37] further improved these models by incorporating invertible 1×11\times 1 convolutions, which led to better performance in image generation. Flow++ [29] enhanced expressiveness by integrating attention mechanisms. iResNet [2] showed that standard ResNet architectures [28] could be made invertible by adding normalization steps. Additionally, normalizing flows have been instrumental in improving Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) [38] by enabling more flexible posteriors [63, 76], and in diffusion models [62] by introducing flexible nonlinear drift and diffusion terms [36]. However, these approaches often require carefully designed and restrictive architectures, which can hinder scalability.

Continuous Normalizing Flows

Neural Ordinary Differential Equations [11] reinterpret the ResNet architecture as a deterministic ODE in the continuous-time limit, which naturally extends to the concept of Continuous Normalizing Flows. In this setting, invertibility is guaranteed, and the Jacobian determinant reduces to the trace of the Jacobian. The adjoint method, based on Pontryagin’s Maximum Principle [54], enables efficient gradient computation with constant memory requirements. FFJORD [24] made Jacobian trace estimation more efficient by using Hutchinson’s estimator [33]. Despite these advances, such models can be numerically unstable during training and sampling, as discussed in [79, 43]. Their expressiveness can be further increased by introducing auxiliary variables [18, 9].

Autoregressive Normalizing Flows

There has also been considerable progress in combining normalizing flows with autoregressive models. IAF [39] proposed dimension-wise affine transformations conditioned on previous dimensions for variational inference, while MAF [50] utilized the MADE [20] architecture to realize invertible mappings via autoregressive transformations. Neural autoregressive flow [32] replaced the affine transformation in MAF with a monotonic neural network per dimension, increasing expressiveness at the expense of analytical invertibility. T-NAF [52] extended NAF by employing a single autoregressive Transformer. Block Neural Autoregressive Flow [8] instead fits an end-to-end autoregressive monotonic neural network, as opposed to NAF’s dimension-wise approach, but also loses analytical invertibility.

Probability Flow in Diffusion

Diffusion models [60, 30, 62] generate samples by simulating stochastic differential equations. Song et al. [62] introduced a deterministic ODE formulation, known as scoreflow [61], as a counterpart to the stochastic process. This scoreflow can be viewed as a special case of continuous normalizing flows, where the learned score and base drift are combined into a new drift term. However, Lu et al. [46] showed that the standard training objective in diffusion models, which is based on a first-order score approximation, does not maximize the likelihood for the scoreflow.

Diffusion models, other generative models

Diffusion models [30, 62] have recently emerged as powerful generative models, achieving impressive results. Stable Diffusion [53] and OpenSora [78] have demonstrated the ability of diffusion models to generate extremely high-dimensional data. Other prominent generative models include Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) [38] and Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) [23]. VQ-VAE [65] addresses posterior collapse and achieves strong generative performance, serving as a key component in later latent diffusion models [53]. In the GAN domain, works such as [35, 34, 4] have demonstrated the ability to generate high-resolution images with relatively low inference cost, though training GANs remains challenging due to stability issues [68].

Continuous Diffusion for Discrete Data

A common strategy for modeling discrete data is to operate in a continuous embedding space, adapting continuous diffusion techniques. This enables the use of powerful continuous models, but requires mapping back to the discrete domain. Diffusion-LM [40] applied continuous diffusion to word embeddings, allowing for controllable text generation via gradient-based guidance. Plaid [27] focused on likelihood-based text modeling, jointly optimizing embeddings and model parameters using the VLB, categorical reparameterization, an output prior, a learned conditional likelihood p⁡(x|z0)p(x|z_{0}), and self-conditioning. CDCD [15] used a probability flow ODE on embeddings, employing score interpolation to jointly train embeddings and a denoising Transformer with a cross-entropy loss and time warping. Bit Diffusion [12] represented discrete data as continuous "analog bits," incorporating self-conditioning and asymmetric time intervals. While these methods are effective, they rely on continuous relaxations or embeddings, motivating the development of models that operate directly on discrete spaces. Many of these works also explore non-autoregressive, parallel generation approaches [3, 26, 40, 31, 57, 10, 72, 73, 70, 13, 14, 74], in contrast to sequential autoregressive models.

Discrete Diffusion Models

Another line of research focuses on diffusion processes that are inherently defined on discrete state spaces, typically using Markov chains. Building on early work [60, 31], D3PM [1] generalized discrete diffusion by employing various structured transition matrices (such as uniform, absorbing, and Gaussian-like) and training with a hybrid VLB/cross-entropy loss. Campbell et al. [6] extended this to Continuous-Time Markov Chains (CTMCs), deriving a continuous-time ELBO and proposing efficient sampling methods like tau-leaping and predictor-corrector schemes, leveraging factorization for scalability.

Rather than simulating Markov chains directly, some works define score-like quantities for discrete diffusion. The concrete score, given by the ratio of marginal probabilities pt​(𝐲)/pt​(𝐱)p_{t}({\mathbf{y}})/p_{t}({\mathbf{x}}), serves as a discrete analogue to the continuous score [48, 45]. SEDD [45] trained models using a score entropy objective (LD​S​EL_{DSE}) based on this ratio, relating it to the ELBO and employing Tweedie τ\tau-leaping for sampling. Sun et al. [64] introduced categorical ratio matching in a CTMC framework, learning singleton conditionals pt​(xd|𝐱∖d)p_{t}(x^{d}|{\mathbf{x}}^{\setminus d}) with a tractable loss and an analytical reverse sampler. Building on this, Ou et al. [49] showed that for absorbing diffusion, the concrete score decomposes into a time-independent conditional and a time-dependent scalar, simplifying the model (RADD) and leading to the Denoising Cross-Entropy (DCE) loss.

Masked (absorbing) diffusion, which replaces tokens with a special [MASK] token during the forward process, has proven highly effective. MDLM [56] introduced a substitution-based parameterization (SUBS) and derived a simplified Rao-Blackwellized ELBO equivalent to weighted Masked Language Modeling (MLM) losses, enabling generative training of encoder-only models. Shi et al. [58] (MD4) further unified this framework, deriving a simple ELBO with SNR invariance properties akin to continuous diffusion and generalizing to state-dependent masking schedules.

Further advances have refined the parameterization and mechanisms of discrete diffusion. Reparameterized Discrete diffusion Models (RDM) [77] identified a route-and-denoise mechanism, reducing the objective to cross-entropy on noisy tokens and enabling adaptive routing during sampling. Liu et al. [44] proposed Discrete Diffusion with Planned Denoising (DDPD), which factorizes the reverse process into a planner (predicting corruption) and a denoiser, allowing for adaptive sampling via the Gillespie algorithm guided by the planner.

Discrete Flow Matching provides another generalization. Gat et al. [19] defined probability paths interpolating between discrete distributions and derived corresponding probability velocities, analogous to continuous flow matching, yielding a unified sampling theory. [7] formulated discrete flows using CTMCs, learning scores via cross-entropy and enabling flexible inference by adjusting the rate matrix family at test time without retraining, also supporting multimodal generation. Discrete diffusion concepts have also been extended to structured data, such as graphs, as in DiGress [67], which uses specialized noise transitions, auxiliary features, and classifier guidance.
